Two cabinet ministers, Works Minister Fournier and Fisheries Minister Bridges expressed themselves in favour of the present procedure of having parliament deal with divorce eases.

So far as I can see there is no way you can get around the present problem. There is no way you can impose on the people of Quebec something they do not want-
Sir, I did not say on that occasion that I was in favour of the present system, nor for that matter did I say that I was against it, and further, I did not say, "There is no way you can impose on the people of Quebec something they ,do not want." What I did say, and what appears on page 1420 of Hansard of May 10, was as follows; and I quote:
-and so far as I can see at the present time there is no way that you can get around the present system. I am sure there is no desire on the part of any one to impose upon the province of Quebec a court which the majority of the people in that province do not want.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. GLEN (Minister of Mines and Resources) moved:
subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
That a joint committee of the senate and house of commons be appointed to examine and consider the Indian Act, Chapter 98, R.S.C., 1927, and amendments thereto and to suggest such amendments as they may deem advisable, with authority to investigate and report upon Indian administration in general and, in particular, the following matters:
1.	Treaty rights and obligations.
2.	Band membership.
3.	Liability of Indians to pay taxes.
4.	Enfranchisement of Indians both voluntary and involuntary.
5.	Eligibility of Indians to vote at dominion elections.
6.	The encroachment of white persons on Indian reserves.
7.	The operation of Indian day and residential schools.
8.	And any other matter or thing pertaining to the social and economic status of Indians and their advancement, which, in the opinion of such a committee should be incorporated in the revised act.

That the following members be appointed to act on behalf of the House of Commons on the said joint committee, namely, Messrs. Arsenault, Blackmore, Brown, Brunelle, Bryce, Case, Castle-den, Charlton, Farquhar, Gariepy, Gibson (Comox-Alberni), Glen, Ilarkness, Little, Mac-Nicol, MacLean, Matthews (Brandon), Raymond (Wright), Reid, Richard (Gloucester), Stanfield, Stirling.
_ That a message be sent to the senate requesting their honours to appoint senators to act as members of the senate on the said special joint committee.
That the said committee have power to appoint from its members such subcommittees as may be deemed advisable or necessary to deal with specific phases of the problem aforesaid with power to call for persons, papers and records, to examine witnesses under oath and to print such materials from day to day as may be ordered by the committee for the use of the committee and members of the House of Commons and the Senate.
That the said committee shall report from time to time and that the provisions of standing order 65 limiting the number of members on special committees be suspended in relation thereto and that a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their honours therewith.
He said; The motion before the house in a very real sense is self-explanatory. It represents the initial step toward a review by a committee of parliament of the legislation relating to the administration of Indian affairs, usually referred to as the Indian Act. It is, in the judgment of the government, highly desirable, one might almost say imperative, before a revision of the Indian Act is undertaken, certainly before the revised act is submitted to the house, that existing legislation, together with amendments that may be deemed necessary, be carefully studied not only from the point of view of the government and the taxpayer, but also from the point of view of the Indian, and in the light of his present-day needs.
Requests-I might almost say, demands- for this inquiry have come to us from representative groups of Indians, from church authorities, and from groups of citizens who over a period of years have displayed an active interest in the advancement of the Indian population of this country. It was at first suggested that a royal commission be appointed to investigate and report upon Indian treaty rights, the taxation of Indians employed off reserves, the right of the Indian to have representation in parliament, the Indian educational system, and a number of other matters. While the government from the outset conceded that the revision of the act was overdue and that the requests for an inquiry were not unreasonable, it was not an easy matter to decide on the exact procedure that would be likely to bring about the best results.

Indian Affairs-Joint Committee
As I intimated to the house at the last session, I had at that time an open mind on the question as to whether a royal commission or a committee of parliament would serve best the purpose we had in mind. May I remind the house that the welfare of the Indian is the sole responsibility of the federal government. It is not a responsibility shared by the government with the provinces. This expression of opinion applies particularly to the enactment of legislation relating to Indian affairs.
After careful consideration the government reached the decision that a committee such as the one now proposed is in strict conformity with sound parliamentary practice. The task of undertaking a thorough undertaking of the Indian and his needs is, in our judgment, a definite responsibility of parliament and one that we should not seek to evade.
It is not my intention to enter into a lengthy discussion of the resolution before us at this stage. The terms of reference, if I may refer to them as such, are not designed to restrict in any way the scope or the character of the inquiry. They are presented in the form in which they appear rather for the purpose of emphasis. It is the desire of the government that the work of the committee should be as thorough, as comprehensive and as searching as it is possible to make it. With tips thought in mind we shall do everything possible to have Indians and responsible citizens representing Indians appear as witnesses. We are not only willing but anxious to have the best counsel and advice that can be obtained from Indians and from citizens who will make respresentations on their behalf.
When I took part in the discussion of a motion to grant old age pensions to Indians at the last session I expressed the opinion that the dissatisfaction which appeared to exist among Indians was in the main attributable to certain causes which are readily ascertainable. May I be permitted to summarize what I said at the time?
I would not be fair to the house, however, if I sought to create an impression that any difficulties which exist in the administration of Indian affairs were due in whole or even in part to our lack of information as a government on existing conditions among the Indians. I am rather convinced that the measure of economy insisted upon by the Canadian taxpayer from 1929 to the outbreak of war, the demands of the war itself, more rigid enforcement on the part of provincial governments of laws relating to hunting, trapping and fishincr. and the gradual encroachment of white citizens into areas where lands, although the property of the provinces, nominally at least had been recognized as exclusive Indian hunting and trapping areas, in the main have contributed to the conditions now confronting us. In any event the need for
a comprehensive programme based on the immediate and future needs of the Indian population is becoming increasingly apparent.
The return of the natural resources to the prairie provinces and the administration of the lands by the provincial governments for which provision was made in the terms of the agreements entered into at that time, imposed greater restrictions on a number of Indians engaged in hunting and trapping. The house will be interested to learn that prior to the return of the natural resources to the provinces, a survey in 1939 indicated that over
30,000	licences were issued to white trappers in that year throughout the various provinces and territories, excluding the maritimes, while not more than 15,000 licences had been granted to Indian trappers. The fact is that as the population of the country steadily increases, and the demands on the part of the citizens for land and other rights multiply, the Indian becomes subject to keener competition in fields of endeavour where for centuries he enjoyed a virtual monopoly.
It would appear that we have reached a stage in our development as a nation when economic conditions will force us to do one of two things: (1) purchase at public expense the additional lands and additional hunting and trapping rights for an Indian population of 128,000, increasing at the rate of 1,500 a year; or, (2) decide on an educational and welfare programme that will fit and equip the Indian to enter into competition with the white man not only in hunting and trapping but in agriculture and in the industrial life of the nation. While I have no desire to indulge in over-simplification; while I realize that there are many issues involved in the proposal before us, nevertheless I feel that we have here the crux of what is usually referred to as the Indian problem. I find it difficult to convince myself that an extending Indian reserve system, imposing controls and wardships and reducing Indian responsibility to the minimum, would be or could be in the interests of these people.
The educational and welfare programme to which I have referred cannot, in the nature of things, accomplish much overnight. Nor should it be aimed at making the Indian into a white man. The Indian, as I see it, should retain and develop many of his native characteristics, and should ultimately assume the full rights and responsibilities of democratic citizenship.
I should like, with your permission, to read into the record for the benefit of the members of the committee particularly, a brief historical summary of Indian administration in this country.

Indian Affairs-Joint Committee
Since the inception of British rule in North America the Indians have been regarded as a special and separate responsibility of government. From the time of the first British settlements in New England the title of the Indians to lands occupied by them was conceded and compensation was made to them for the surrender of their hunting grounds. The crown has always reserved to itself the exclusive right to treat with the Indians for the surrender of their lands, and this rule, confirmed by the royal proclamation of October 7, 1763, is still adhered to. In 1670, during the reign of Charles II, instructions were given to the governors of the colonies which, among other matters, directed that Indians who desired to place themselves under British rule should be well received and protected. There are still of record numerous agreements and treaties, dating back as far as the year 1664, made by the British with the Indians of New England, while Canada was still under French government. Later it was found necessary to establish an office devoted solely to the administration of Indian affairs, and in 1755 Sir William Johnson was appointed Indian superintendent with headquarters in the Mohawk valley country of the Six Nations confederacy in what is now the state of New York. Following the- revolution, the office was removed to Canada and the title of the position was changed to superintendent general of Indian affairs. From that time on a continuing administrative organization has been maintained for the protection and advancement of the Indian population. At the end of the eighteenth and the beginning of the nineteenth century the department was divided. The office of the superintendent general and the secretary of the department was established in Montreal, and that of the deupty superintendent general and assistant secretary, at Fort George, Niagara; and by a general order of May 13,1816, the management of Indian affairs was placed under the control of the commander of the forces in the British North American provinces.
By another general order of April 13, 1830, the management of Indian affairs in Upper Canada was placed under Sir John Colborne, lieutenant governor for that province, while that in Lower Canada remained under military control. In 1830, by order of His Majesty's government, the Indian department in Upper Canada was separated from that of Lower Canada, the former being placed under His Excellency Sir John Colborne, with Colonel Sir James Givins as chief superintendent for the province. The department in Lower Canada was placed under the control of the military secretary at Quebec who at that time
rMr. Glen.]
was Lieutenant Colonel Couper, and Lieutenant Colonel D. C. Napier was removed to the military secretary's office to act as secretary, with the pay and allowances of superintendent.
After the Act of Union of 1840, the head office of the Department of Indian Affairs, now united, continued to be at the seat of government, which under the old province of Canada was moved from one place to another. Until 1860 the imperial government was responsible for the management and expense of Indian affairs, but in that year it was decided that the province of Canada should assume this charge. By the act 23 Victoria, chapter 151, entitled "An Act respecting the management of the Indian lands and property", the management of Indian affairs was brought under the control of the Crown Lands Department from July 1, 1860, the commissioner of crown lands being from that date chief superintendent of Indian affairs.
After confederation the administration of Indian affairs, which had been under the management of the several provinces, came under the control of the Dominion of Canada, by the British North America Act, "powers of the parliament", dominion, section 91, subsection 24, "Indians, and Lands Reserved for the Indians". Pursuant to this authority the dominion parliament enacted various legislation concerning Indians, which was first consolidated in a single act, as it still is, in 1876.
Immediately following confederation, Indian Affairs was attached to the Department of the Secretary of State, and in 1873, when the Department of the Interior was created, Indian Affairs was attached to it as the Indian branch. In 1880 the Indian Act was again consolidated, and it was provided, section 4:
There shall be a department of the civil service of Canada to be called the Department of Indian Affairs, over which the superintendent general of Indian affairs shall preside.
Chapter 28, 43, Victoria, 1880. Accordingly, Indian Affairs became a separate department and remained so until December 1, 1936, when by the mines and resources act it became the Indian Affairs branch of the newly-created Department of Mines and Resources. It is interesting to note that when the department of Indian Affairs was created in 1880 it comprised twenty-three officers at headquarters and one hundred in the field. To-day the Indian Affairs branch has a staff of about 70 at headquarters and 700 in the field. In addition, there is the Indian health service recently transferred to the Department of National Health and Welfare. These services employ a

Indian Affairs-Joint Committee
staff of approximately 600, including physicians, nurses, and other employees, with sixteen hospitals.
In 1880 the total expenditure from parliamentary vote for Indians was, in round figures, $500,000. During the fiscal year ended March 31, 1945-last year-it was, exclusive of family allowance payments, approximately $6,000,000. This growth in personnel and expenditures represents increased and extended services to the Indians.
There are at present 2,000 Indian reserves, varying in size from a few acres to five hundred square miles. The group unit of Indian population is the "band", which means a body of Indians having lands or funds in common held in trust for them by the crown. There are six hundred of these bands, varying in size from a single family to more than 5,000 souls.
The unit of field administration is the Indian agency in charge of a resident local official, the Indian agent. At this date there are ninety-eight of these agencies. Closely connected with the Indian agency organization is the Indian school system, comprising 75 residential and 258 Indian day schools. These are operated by the department in conjunction with the leading religious denominations. At many of the agencies there are farming instructors, and in a number of localities the Indians receive supervision in specialized pursuits such as fur development projects, handicrafts and other activities.
The house will be interested and perhaps a little surprised to learn that the Indian Act of 1880, with amendments made from time to time, is still in effect. It has not been the subject of a general revision since that year. The basis of this act, or indeed of all Indian legislation and policy under British government in North America, is the special protection of the Indian in his person, his property, his advancement and his general well-being. The Indian is subject to certain restrictions but enjoys a measure of local selfgovernment under the act. Those who do not wish to remain under Indian status may, on their own application if found qualified, be enfranchised by the governor in council, whereupon they cease to be Indians under the law and acquire full citizenship.
In passing, I may say that many Indians are taking advantage of that provision. Only last Tuesday I signed fifteen orders enfranchising Indians.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext: Is the act of 1880, together with subsequent amendments, consolidated?

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
Yes. We have it here; it is consolidated for office purposes only. All the provisions of the act together with the amendments are here. A rough draft of the revised act will be submitted to the committee during the course of its deliberations. This rough draft represents an attempt on the part of the officials of the Indian Affairs branch to bring existing legislation more into accord with the needs of the Indians and present-day tendencies. I am personally of the opinion, however, that before the draft is considered the committee will wish to hear a comparatively large number of witnesses who will be anxious to make representations and express points of view. The task is assuredly not an easy one. If approached in the right spirit, however, as I am sure it will be, the results should be gratifying and encouraging to the white citizen and the Indian alike.
Finally, let me say that while a great deal of criticism has been directed against Indian administration during the last twenty-five years or so, there is a brighter side to this picture, the significance of which should not be overlooked. In numbers the race is increasing; in educational effort the Indian is developing, slowly perhaps, but nevertheless developing toward a better acquaintance with the ways of the white race. His blood is becoming steadily more mixed, which, in fact, points toward ultimate assimilation. It is possible, in my judgment, to say that too much emphasis has been frequently placed upon the fancied injustice of requiring the Indian to conform to changing conditions. In the last analysis it is both just and expedient to help the Indian to adjust himself to these conditions. It is neither necessary nor merciful in the long run to encourage him perpetually to continue in a state of backwardness or semi-backwardness. Nevertheless, as I have already indicated, the process of assimilation cannot be unduly hurried, nor must it be rushed. Time, we are told, heals all wounds, and in this healing process the soars of race tension, conflict and misunderstanding will, I feel sure, disappear.
Judging by the expressions of opinion that have been given not only in this house but all over the country, showing an interest in Indian affairs, I am sure the house will agree that this resolution is the first step to be taken, namely, the appointment of a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate. In that committee, which will have the revised amendments suggested by the Indian Affairs branch, and where witnesses from all over the country who may desire to express opinions and give information to the
Indian Affairs-Joint Committee

committee, will be heard, I am satisfied that the work, which seems momentous in the beginning may prove not so difficult in the end. I believe that out of this committee will come legislation and suggestions in administration which will help the development of the Indian, which I am sure is the desire of the house. For that reason I am moving this motion, hoping that the house will see fit to pass it and that the committee will be set up accordingly.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
As one who for many years has been interested in the study of Indian affairs and of all that pertains to the advancement of the Indian, I rise not to delay but to support the principles of the resolution as enunciated by the minister. I believe that the present minister is the first minister who has planned to inquire in a big way into every possible means of improving the whole Indian picture in Canada. With [DOT]that objective of the minister-and I am sure in this I am speaking for other hon. members of this house-I am in hearty accord.
I have often wondered why it was that the Indians of Canada, who have been so long under the control of the white man, have not advanced as rapidly as have the Maoris of New Zealand and even the coloured races in South Africa. In New Zealand the Maoris now have a number of representatives in the parliament of that country, and the same is true of South Africa. I am not sure whether the coloured people of South Africa themselves sit in the South African parliament. My memory is that they elect white people to represent them in parliament, and that these white representatives of the South African coloured races speak for them. For that reason I have wondered why our so-called coloured native race'-they are of a reddish or copper colour-have not advanced as far as the native races of the countries to which I have just referred. They have long been under the control of the white man. First they were under the control of the British-I am now speaking of the British in New York-under Sir William Johnson, the great administrator, and later under his son, Sir John Johnson. In Canada I believe Sir John Johnson was the first Indian administrator. If I may interject a suggestion I should like the minister to go down to Williamstown in the county of Glengarry some day where the first Indian administration house was built by Sir John Johnson. His house is still standing. It has passed out of the hands of the Johnson family, but I think it would be a fine gesture on Canada's part to purchase Sir John Johnson's

old house, if it is for sale, and set it up as a museum of, Indian relics in that part of Canada.
As I said at the beginning, I have been intensely interested' in Indian affairs over a long period of time. My interest ha-s necessitated some travel and impelled me to visit many reservations. In the course of these journeys to the reservations I would first seek out the chief of the immediate band or branch on whose reservation I then was to . ascertain from him all I could and to inquire into what improvements could be made in Indian administration. From what the minister has said, I have no doubt that he intends to call to the committee the main chiefs, or those who represent them, of the various bands.
I myself have paid many visits to the Six Nations in the riding of the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Charlton) and that of the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn). In those ridings are the remnants of the famous Six Nations. I am not just sure how many of the branches came to Brant and Haldimand, but certainly the Mohawks did. The Oneidas did and the Muncies went a little farther west in the county of Elgin and are still there. The Delawares were not of the Six Nations. They settled further west at Moraviantown in Kent. I believe there are Senecas, Oneidas, Onon-dagas and Mohawks in Brant. They were of the famous Iroquois tribe.
I hope that the outcome of the committee's investigation will result in a much greater advancement of Indian life along the line, economically, educationally and in a business way, so that we as a parliament may be the means of stepping them up to a much higher level than they occupy to-day. In my travels I have found a great difference as between various reserves in the advancement of the Indian tribes. As far as I recall, the Iroquois in Brant and Haldimand are perhaps more advanced than any other Indians in Canada, though it may be that some of the tribes in Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia have also made considerable advances, because they have been long associated with white men. If we compare what they have achieved with what has been achieved by members of the coloured race who have come to Canada, principally from Jamaica and the southern United States, we have to admit that the coloured race have most assuredly achieved a very great deal in every walk of life. The Indians also have achieved something-although I observe from what the minister has said, not as much as he would like to see.

Indian Affairs-Joint Committee
In this investigation I am quite sure all hon. members of this house, including those serving on the committee, will use their best judgment and seek the best possible advice to draw up recommendations designed to advance the status of our Indians all along the line. I am not going to enter into a detailed discussion at the moment, because I do not think it is necessary. I could say a great deal about the Indians, but that can be done in committee, and if I said very much now I would simply repeat it in the committee later. I feel that I have done my duty by merely rising to support this proposal for the betterment of our Indians. It is high time we did something of this kind; in fact the time is long past when this should have been done. I am not blaming anyone. Having been here for seventeen years I know that almost invariably the Indian estimates come up in the last few hours of a session and are carried so rapidly that nothing can be said to advance the welfare of the Indians, with the exception of perhaps one or two of the principal speeches. So after this investigation is completed I hope much may be done for these native people.
Many Indian chiefs have given me their views on these matters. I have spoken to them all over Canada, as far north as at Arctic Red river; at lake Athabasca; the Norman Indians near where Norman Wells is now; the Stoneys in Alberta; the Fairford River Indians in northern Manitoba, and the Moose Lake Indians, also in northern Manitoba. Perhaps I should not have mentioned any particular bands at all, but now that I have done so 1 should mention the Blackfeet Indians; and in the tribe in the riding of the hon. member for Lethbridge, right in his home town of Card-ston, I met some chiefs of this band, whose name always slips my mind.

speechtext:
That is it. I asked the chief why they called themselves the Bloods, and he replied, "Well, you know when a rich man has a son he is called a young blood. A man who owns a fast race horse calls it a blood. We are an up and coming band of Indians, so we call ourselves the Bloods." That was his explanation as to how they got that name. It would be interesting, I believe, to ascertain the origin of all these Indian names.
Now, Mr. Speaker, following the example of the minister in proposing this resolution, I merely wish to repeat that I am heartily in accord with the proposal and sincerely hope that' it will result in a great advancement of the Indians all along the line so that they may take their place among the white men who owe so much to them. We have taken
away so much from them that we should try our best to advance their interests now. We might even consider having representatives of the Indians sitting in this house, just as the Maoris have in New Zealand. That is something which should be kept in mind in this connection. '	^

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
First I should like to congratulate the minister, who is new in this department and who I think is tackling this job in a way that should bring success. I am glad he is setting up this committee to give all the members of the House of Commons an opportunity to help in the revision of the whole Indian Act. It is a big job, and I think those who have made any study whatever of the Indian problem will realize what a tremendous task lies ahead. For instance, the committee has to revise treaty rights and obligations. The treaties alone require a tremendous amount of study. The committee also will have to consider band membership, the liability of Indians, the encroachment of white persons on Indian reserves, and so on. During the last few months I have done quite a lot of reading on the history of the Indians, and I find that the whole story of the treatment of the Indians by the white men has been one of exploitation all the way through. Not long ago I was talking to an Indian, who said, "The white man is very greedy. He grabs this and he grabs that," and that is so. Whenever the Indians had a reserve that included good farm land, the white man found a way of getting them to take inferior land, and it has been the same with timber. There were good timber berths on some of the Indian lands, and the white man found ways and means of getting the Indians to give up that timber. So I say it will be a tremendous job to look through these old treaties and old deeds of gift to find out just what the Indians have had to put up with.
I rise to-day more particularly to give the committee a little encouragement. I know some people have said the Indian is no good, that you cannot make anything out of him. During the Easter recess I had an opportunity to go to the Six Nations Indian reserve just south of Brantford, and I would not have missed that trip for anything. There I found very highly civilized, well-educated, cultured Indians, and I want to say something about some of the things I saw. In the first place I believe the whole reserve would average up pretty well as a farming community with any community of white people. They have eleven day-schools on this reserve. All the teachers are Indians, most of whom were educated on the reserve and who then went on further

Indian Affairs-Joint Committee
with their education. They have fourteen Indian teachers teaching the Indian children. I looked at their work and spoke to one of the teachers, and I believe the work those children were doing would compare favourably with the work done in any of the white schools. They have their own agricultural society. They have a very neat little town, Oshweken, on the outskirts of which they have their own agricultural grounds. Those grounds are neat, as everything else in connection with that reserve is neat. When you enter the agricultural grounds you go through a double arch gate, and inside to the right you find a recreation hall. I think these Indian teachers have done a wonderful work in preparing the young people of the reservation for citizenship. The recreation hall is large enough to permit the playing of basketball and softball. The young people meet twice a week and they can play these games. They are taught archery and many other things. They even have an orchestra of eighteen or twenty pieces, and also several small bands. They have a seed cleaning plant which is capable of cleaning all the seed used on the reservation.
I asked them how they were making out as far as higher education was concerned and they told me that in a number of the schools they teach first year high school but that quite a number have gone on to take higher education. I asked how many had entered the professions and they gave me a list. There is a Doctor T. J. Jamieson who is practising medicine at the present time in Detroit. Doctor F. A. Johnson is an eye specialist in Akron, Ohio. D. J. Smith, B.S.A., is in New Zealand. Doctor E. Jamieson is a science teacher in North Toronto collegiate. Doctor T. A. Miller is a homeopath specialist in tuberculosis. A lawyer named Norman Lickers is practising in Brantford. A very interesting person is Doctor Minnie S. Buerk. Doctor Buerk first graduated in Canada as a nurse. She went to the United States and married a doctor in Detroit. About a year and a half later her husband died, and she then went to the university there and took a course in medicine. She is now practising in Detroit. Another interesting person of whom I heard was a girl who had also graduated as a nurse in Canada. She went to the United States and was employed to take care of a sub-normal son of the Sears family

the Sears-Roebuck people. This boy could hardly speak and had little use of his hands. This girl taught the boy not only to speak, but also to read and write and how to use his hands. Eventually she married one of the members of the Sears family.

Three parsons graduated from these schools, one of them Reverend Jeno Porter, who broadcasts every Sunday from Brantford. I think it would be very interesting for any hon. member who happened to be in that vicinity to visit this reserve. It is an illuminating illustration of what can be done with the Indians. As I said before, some people have an idea that you cannot make anything out of an Indian. I admit that at times it may seem a big job, but there is no doubt that there are individuals on every reserve who have the capacity to learn, and they should be given every opportunity to get an education.
We have slipped up badly in the education of our Indians. Many of the reserves depend entirely upon residential schools. I have nothing against the residential school, because I know it is doing a lot of good work, but a large percentage of the children on some of the reserves do not go to school because there are no day schools. Last winter, speaking to a band of Indians, I told them that the Indians themselves must accept some of the responsibility of educating their people. I told them that they would have to do what the white people were doing, that is, have compulsory education so that their children would have to go to school.
I think we shall have to get the cooperation of the Indians before we can make much headway with their education. I suggest to the minister that when he is choosing men who are to be agents or teachers, he should not select them in a haphazard manner. They should be chosen for their special qualifications, and the main qualification should be an understanding of the Indian and an ability to get the Indian to cooperate with them.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am entirely in favour of the terms and implications of this resolution, and I wish to compliment the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) upon having brought the matter up for discussion in the House of Commons. I believe a similar discussion was originated last year by a private member's resolution, and some hon. members were afraid that the question might be left in abeyance. We are glad indeed to see this demonstration of the alertness of the minister and his department.
I am glad that the resolution calls for the setting up of a committee of members of parliament rather than a royal commission. I am not against royal commissions as such; often they have done splendid work, but in dealing with a question of this kind, in which departments of government are directly

Indian Affairs-Joint Committee
concerned and in connection with which there is no legal point involved, I believe the best procedure is to set up a committee composed of members of parliament.
If you read the names of the hon. members comprising the committee you will see that they come from every part of Canada. Many of them are familiar not only with their own local Indian problems but also with problems affecting Indians generally across the country. Again I should like to compliment the minister upon having taken action for the appointment of the committee. Royal commissions have done good work in the past, but if we are to reach practical conclusions I do not think there is any better way of doing so under our parliamentary system than to set up a committee of this kind.
I may be a little disappointed personally because I have not been named as a member of the committee, but even though I had been named it might have been impossible for me to attend its sessions, because I hope that the external affairs committee will soon begin to sit and I expect to be quite busy there; besides I have to attend other committees.
I happen to represent a section of the country which takes in the James Bay area in which there is a large Indian population. There are local problems to be faced, and there are problems national in character. I know that all of them will be dealt with by this committee in a proper and practical way.
The committee should not be satisfied with sitting in Ottawa only. Although it might take a lot of time, I think the committee should visit the different centres of Indian population from the Atlantic to the Pacific-and I am referring particularly to my own section. I hope the committee will find it possible to visit the Indian population at Moosonee, Moose Factory, Fort George and Fort Albany. I realize that the Indian Affairs branch has been giving a good deal of attention to these problems and spending considerable money, with fruitful results, but I think it would be worth while if the members of the committee could visit the Indians. It might cost a little more, but it would be money well spent.
I would not for a moment attempt to dictate or give direction to the chairman or members of the committee, but I do hope that my suggestion in this regard will be implemented. It would be a wonderful way to get to the root of the problem. I was greatly enlightened, although I had thought I knew something about the Indian problem, by the speeches of hon. members of the C.C.F. and Progressive Conservative parties on this subject 63260-92
in present and past sessions. The member for Comox-Alberni gave a most interesting account of the Indian people, describing their fine qualities and festivities and customs, which I am sure were a revelation not only to the members of parliament but to the people of Canada generally.
I hope that the committee will visit every section of our Indian population and will consider the Indian problem not only in itself but also as it is related to Canada as a whole. The committee will have a lot of work to do. I think it will be impossible for them to make a final report this year, but I am sure that the work they do will be well received not only by parliament but by the whole country. It will take much time and involve personal sacrifices. I do not mean that the members should pay their travelling expenses. For a number of years before I was Deputy Speaker of the house I was a member of the war expenditures committee, and when it was first mooted that the committee would travel I thought that the expenses should be borne by the individual members. But it did not take me very long to see that that would be unfair to members of parliament, and so I hope that the principle followed in that case will apply to this committee, because it will have to cover a good deal of territory. The members of the committee may have to go to the Yukon and the northwest territories. They may have to go to the habitats of the Eskimo. Certainly they will have to visit the northern section of my part of the country in order to study the actual conditions on the ground.
It is said that the Indians, generally speaking, do not mix with the white population. That does not hold true of my part of the country. I know many full-blooded Indians who do mix with the white population, and to their benefit. I know full-blooded -Indians who are succeeding in the professions, and I hope that the educational system for the Indians will make it possible for them to become scientific agriculturists, technicians and craftsmen of various kinds. Some of the Indians are excellent doctors, and others good dentists. It would not be doing justice to the Indians, with all their natural talents, to keep them on their reserves and expect them always to earn their living by hunting and trapping. Many of the younger men have gone into the outside world, particularly those who have enlisted or attended our public and high schools. They are proud of the calling of their forefathers, but their horizons have widened and many of them have become enterprising co-citizens of the white popula-



Indian Affairs-Joint Committee
tion in our section of the country. I am convinced, however, that contact with the white man has not- often been of benefit to the Indians. It has disturbed, in many, their way of living, and means must be found of maintaining the integrity of the Indians' own habitat.
The Ontario government about eight years ago set aside a large section of territory south of James bay, embracing thousands of square miles where the timber is not very heavy, to develop beaver, otter and mink. I have been told that ten or twelve years from now there will be sufficient of that wild game in that territory to give a living to at least ten thousand Indians, and some of the white population too. A scheme of that kind should be enlarged, and I hope the committee will find it possible to recommend the setting aside of thousands of square miles which should be left entirely to the Indians where they can make a living by hunting and trapping. To that they are entitled, and they should be assisted and encouraged by a scheme of that sort. The time has arrived when the demarcation line should be withdrawn between federal and provincial activities and when schemes such as I have mentioned should be instituted in many sections of northern Canada. I am an optimist by nature. I implicitly believe in our wonderful country and its future. As we have heard many times on the floor of the house, -and read in the press, it is a land with wide open spaces, no doubt designed by Providence to remain as such for all time to come. Nevertheless there are ways of raising the standards of the Indians and providing them with fruitful employment, and one industry to which they are peculiarly adapted is fur raising. The furs we produce in the northern section of Canada command a premium in the world market. Any fur coming from my section of the country, from around James bay or Hudson bay, whether it be white fox, otter, beaver or mink, commands a higher price than furs from any other part of the world except northern Russia. A scheme such as the Ontario government has started for the raising of these fur-bearing animals will not only be helpful to the Indians in providing them with employment and a living, but in time to come will be of benefit to the provincial and federal treasuries as well. The scheme will not run into millions of dollars but into hundreds of thousands, and in a few years will be self-sustaining. I should like to see the committee recommend the setting aside and helping the development of areas on the shores of Hudson bay and James 
bay and across northern Ontario, Quebec and Manitoba such as the Ontario government has started.
There is one other thing I should like to mention. On account of the great distances, the Indians often are deprived of hospital accommodation for days and weeks, and I was therefore glad to see the other day that an air line was to be established from Moosonee to Cochrane, Timmins and Haileybury. That will help -to relieve the situation, because these poor Indians follow their trap lines at the risk of life and limb and have to face all the hazards of climate. Tuberculosis is rampant among them, and sanitary conditions are not always what they should be. Often a sore will develop into cancer or some other disease, and so there must be rapid transit to bring those who need it out to civilization for prompt medical attention.
I do not know whether my information is correct, but I have been told that it is the intention of the government to build a large hospital in the James bay section. I believe it was in the year 1928 that I had the good fortune to see an Indian hospital built next to the municipal hospital in Cochrane. It gave fine service to the Indian population. They came to it from the east and west on the transcontinental line, and also from the north and south of our section; but after a number of years the Indian department decided, I believe seven years ago, to close that institution and turn it over to our own hospital. The service was maintained in the same way except that the local hospital was paid so much per patient. But that has not given the necessary service to the Indians. I do not know how correct my information is, but I understand that the department intends to build a fairly large hospital at Moosonee or Moose .Factory. I have no right to dictate to the department, but speaking as one who knows the local and regional situation I fervently hope it will be found possible for the department to build that-hospital in Cochrane. I am not speaking from the point of' view of home politics. The question is away above any political considerations, and I commend the hon. members who have spoken for avoiding political criticisms. But my advice is based on several reasons. First, a large section of our Indian population starts from the shores of the Hudson bay and spreads as far as Amos on the Transcontinental. We have a large section in Matagami that spend most of their summer there, and also at Algoma and west to the town of Hearst on the Canadian National. I know the question comes to mind, what

Indian Affairs-Joint Committee
will become of the Indians of the Hudson bay and James bay sections? It may be found necessary in order to give the best service to that area to have an air service from the Moose bay section and Fort George to that hospital in Cochrane.
I am leaving these thoughts for thorough study and consideration by the minister and officials of his department. They have always been receptive of any practical suggestions I have placed before them, and I know that the permanent heads of this department and the ministers themselves have always wanted to play fair with this class of our population.
While Canada may not have done for the Indians all that we could have wished her to do, she has done better than most other countries. At least we consider them as human beings; the policy has not been one of extermination, but of preservation, of advancement, and of trying to do the best we could with them.
There are two matters referred to in the motion which I should like briefly to mention. First, section 5, eligibility of Indians to vote at dominion elections. Personally I believe that the vote should be accorded to our Indian population. If it were necessary that any citizens in order to vote should have an intelligence test, I am convinced that ninety-five if not ninety-nine per cent of our Indian population could pass that test. For our Indians to hew a living out of the northern sections of our country in districts like the Hudson bay and James bay, to face the climatic conditions involved in fur trapping, and successfully carry on that pursuit, requires much enterprise, initiative, courage and intelligence. The election act as it stands is a baffling piece of legislation. It is perfectly right, no doubt, that the franchise should be extended to Indians who enlisted in world wars I and II, and to their families, but you would be surprised at the reaction of the average Indian when he sees that one of his relatives has the right to vote but that he is denied the vote because, although he wished to do so, for some reason he was unable to enlist. I hope this anomaly will be rectified, because I do not believe in making distinctions between various classes of people. If you allow one section to vote and debar another section, you invite and are bound to have criticisms which are entirely warranted.
I would refer also to paragraph 6, the encroachment of white persons on Indian reserves, I hope members of the committee will study this question thoroughly. No doubt our civilization and the work of our missionaries have brought much blessing to the Indian 63260-92i
population, but at times there is also resentment in the hearts of many Indians at the hardships which have been caused them by a few so-called white people-white in name only, not in respect of their behaviour and conduct to. the Indian people. The law could be so defined that the Indians Shall have exclusive rights in most parts of their own territory, and they shall be protected from any depredation or violation, of the things they cherish. After all, they have maintained their own civilization, their own way of living, and all of us who have any acquaintance with them know how sincere and honest they are. Anyone who has hunted in my own section will have seen along the trails some caches containing meat, and Indian after Indian will tell you that never under any circumstances, unless threatened with starvation, has a single pound of that meat been stolen by the Indians themselves. They would rather suffer than take food which has been placed there for the use of people in need of it. They have some wonderful qualities; they have also resentment in their hearts at the depredations and the temptations which they have suffered at the 'hands of people who are bent upon exploiting them. At this point, as one who knows something of the activities of the Hudson's Bay company and Revillon Freres, may I say that if you go to the Hudson bay-where Revillon Freres are not located at this time-you will see people at the head of those posts working with the Indians, playing the game with them in every way. But sometimes outsiders disturb the peace of mind of the Indians and rob them of the fruits of their activities.
I wish again to compliment the minister upon having presented this motion. I know that splendid and lasting results will be accomplished. We do not need to be impatient. It is a complex question, and it shows the fine spirit of our parliament that, in a matter in which, perhaps, very few votes are involved, there is not one of us but who, for reasons of humanitarianism, wants to relieve these people of sickness and suffering, to remedy the lack of hospitalization and provide proper education and a place in our national life. When it comes to craftsmanship and education-, the department has done wonderful work. Modern methods of trapping, fishing and knitting are taught to our Indians. So the situation at the present time is not bad, but, in the words of the minister, it can be improved. In trying to do this through the work of the committee, pursuant to the directive given by the minister himself, I am positive that our country, which can be proud

Indian Affairs-Joint Committee
to some extent of its past record in dealing with the Indian population, will have even more reason for pride when the recommendations of the committee now being formed have been implemented.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
May I congratulate the minister at the outset upon bringing in this motion, and may I also congratulate him on being the first minister for a good many years who has taken enough interest in this particular branch of his department to desire a thorough housecleaning. However good may be the record of the Indian department-and I think all must concede that it has many good qualities-there certainly must be room for improvement. The minister has adopted one of the means of determining what might be that room for improvement and what measures might appropriately be undertaken to effect the necessary changes. Out in my territory the people feel that there should have been a royal commission instead of a parliamentary committee, and a good many reasons have been advanced for this. The fine programme which- the member for Cochrane (Mr. Bra-dette) outlined for this committee's activities would indicate that probably the committee will be called upon to do such an excellent, such a thorough job as might leave no real demand for a commission. We might be able to do all the work that a commission could do. But those in my territory who advocate a commission point to the fact that the members of a committee of parliament, no matter how wisely that committee may be chosen, will hardly have representatives of the Indians themselves on the personnel of the organization. They feel that certainly there should have been Indian organizations represented, and if we had had a royal commission it would have been a simple matter to include among the personnel several outstanding chiefs and leaders across the country. They point out that it will be exceedingly difficult for a House of Commons committee to do the necessary travelling.
I was almost alarmed at the picture which the member for Cochrane painted. I am wondering how we are going to take care of all the work that requires to be done here and at the same time do the travelling which that member has outlined for us. However, I am certainly in favour of doing everything possible to ensure a thorough job on this question.
I believe we should see what the different tribes do, the conditions under which they live. My own limited experience with Indians has shown me that the conditions under which they live vary widely from tribe to tribe.

Consequently it looks to me as if, unless we see a good many of them in their living conditions, it will be difficult for us to be realistic in any decision we arrive at.
It is not going to be possible for us to hear all the witnesses we ought to hear unless we do a good deal of travelling. This would argue the advisability of having a royal commission rather than a parliamentary committee. The expenses would probably have been less if we had had a royal commission. I am not prepared at the moment to pronounce on that whole question. The thoroughness with which we go into the task will require, I believe, more than a parliamentary committee will be able to rise to.
I do not want to be dubious about the matter, but this has given us one of the reasons why there should have been a royal commission. Everyone suspects a parliamentary committee of having a certain amount of party bias, no matter how well the committee may do its work-at any rate everyone does outside parliament. If we had a royal commission, however, it would be possible to remove all suspicion of anything like party bias in dealing with the question.
We must grant, I believe, that there is a good deal of room for improvement. The Indians in my constituency, in the Blood Indian reserve, read the fine remarks made with reference to Indians being wards of the nation, and they laugh a mirthless laugh. They fail to see how the treatment that has been accorded them can in any way justify the expression "wards of the nation". They feel that they have had to do things in the hard way, and quite often it has been a case "root hog, or die", and they felt that they were close to dying.
There are several sections of the Indian act which the people in my area feel should be improved. They are of the opinion that section 18 should be amended. I will not go into details to show in what respect it should be amended, but the idea is that there is too njuch dictatorial power exercised in the enforcement of that section. The Indians believe that the chiefs and counsellors ought to have adequate pay. Not very long ago several chiefs were in my home from the Blood Indian reserve and were pointing out to me what an expensive business it was being a chief or a counsellor, how far they had to travel on the reserve to hear the problems they were called upon to decide. One of them said to me, "You member of parliament and it cost you a lot of money to travel; I chief and I get no money but I have to travel too." That I felt was a sound observation.

speechtext: What did you say?

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
I said nothing; that seemed to me to be the wisest course. However, I decided that the Indians had a good case. I believe we should make provision for reimbursing these gentlemen for out-ofpocket expenses and any losses they incur as a result of having to neglect their own work to discharge the duties in connection with the position they hold.
The question of military service is one which is exercising the Indians, and a good many of the white people as well. Much attention must be given that question, I should not like to make a pronouncement at the moment as to whether I would favour complete freedom from military service. I submit however that the problem should be carefully studied.
Treaty rights which were granted to the Indians have been in many cases disregarded, as far as I can see. As I recall it, the Indians in my constituency signed in 1877 a treaty known as treaty No. 7. In that treaty there are a good many stipulations which have not been observed. That is not as it should-be. What the reasons are I do not know, but I believe we ought to find out and reaffirm the treaty rights of the Indians. When the Blood Indians and those working with them signed that treaty they believed the white man meant what he said. If the white man did not mean what he said, then we had better see to it that we say it again and mean it.	_
The education of the Indians has occupied a good deal of my attention throughout the last twenty years. I have felt that there was much to be desired on the reservation in my constituency. In the first place-and I am speaking in a purely impersonal way-I find it difficult to see how we can guarantee the Indians an education when we are consigning every Indian on the reserve to become either a Roman Catholic or an Anglican in order to go to school. There are two residential schools, one Roman Catholic and the other Anglican. I have no fault to find with either of these churches, but to say that every Indian should have to become a member of one or the other in order to get an education is to say something which seems reckless and illogical in a country such as Canada. Nevertheless that is the situation. All the education which the Indians obtain in my constituency has been obtained in one or the other of these residential schools, which are definitely religious schools. This is a matter which ought to be considered with great care.
Among our treaty obligations with the Indians was the guarantee that we would educate the Indian, and we are falling far short of giving the Indians on the Blood
Indian Affairs-Joint Committee
Indian reserve what we would call an adequate education. That matter must be probed and a proper remedy prescribed. In my judgment, there should be modern every-day schools.
In my constituency the Blood Indian reservation is a very long stretch of land of many miles. The Indians have to travel a considerable distance. It would not be so bad if they had automobiles, but if they have to travel by team all the way from the remote reaches of the reservation with their children up to the schools and come up occasionally to see _ the children, they are put to exceedingly great inconvenience. It ought to be possible for us to establish day schools on reservations similar to the rural schools which we gave to our white people scattered over the prairies. Therefore it should not be necessary for the Indians to send their children long distances to residential schools for many months at a time.
It is a well-understood principle by all people who give thought to educational matters that education after all is not only just a matter for'the schools to take care of. There are at least three elements involved in education. One of these is the school; certainly another ought to be the home, and the third ought to be the church. Because of the way the children are being educated on the Blood Indian reservation, the home has no chance at all. In fact for over half of the time the children are entirely separated from their parents. Frequently at the end of their education they come back to find the parents do not know them and they do not know the parents, so widely separated-have they become from what they were when they left their homes. This matter ought to be taken care of. So far as I can see the only way to take care of it is to establish day schools at convenient places in the reservations.
Indian parents have a right to the company of their children just as much as white parents have a right to the company of theirs. They have a perfect right to influence their children. When the Indians signed a treaty with us they did not sign away their rights to bring up their children as Indians. They have a perfect right to bring up their children as Indians if they wish to do so.
There is another matter that is rather serious. On the reservation in my constituency many of the parents need the assistance of their boys and girls when they are making hay and doing other work. They need the help of their boys and girls just as much as the white people do; yet the boys are away until they are fifteen or sixteen years of age, and the parents have to get along without

Indian Affairs-Joint Committee
them. That is a matter which ought to be looked into. It is another problem which can be solved only by the use of the everyday school.
It is suggested by some-I am not prepared to suggest it specifically for the Blood Indian reservation because I am not well enough informed on the matter-that there ought to be not only a day school but a semi-residential school here and there on the reservation. It is suggested that it ought to be possible for parents to send their children to residen-' tial schools where they can stay five nights a week and come home for the week-end. Such an arrangement would overcome many of the disadvantages which now obtain by reason of having all the children go to a complete residential school. This is a matter which ought to be given careful consideration by the committee, and upon which recommendations ought to be made.
It is advocated by some that there should be three kinds of schools on reservations where conditions are favourable. There should be a residential school, a semi-residential school here and there where conditions warrant it, and a day school in other places where conditions warrant it.
There is another matter which is receiving considerable attention in some parts of the west. Some Indians desire to send their children to schools which are outside the reservation. In other words, Indians who are better off, more ambitious and progressive desire to send their children to a school in a white community. They find that the children make more progress in those schools, but the cost involved in sending a child to a school outside a reservation is often so great as to render it completely prohibitive, regardless of how desirous the parent may be of giving his children that educational advantage. It is suggested by some that the government ought to be prepared, where children have the opportunity and desire to go to a school in a white community, to pay the tuition and an allowance which would enable the child to have such advantages as adequate laundry service, and so on, which are necessary to enable him to live in that kind of community without being self-conscious, so that he may have the chance to develop. This is a matter which ought to have serious consideration if we are desirous of having the Indians become one with us, as I am sure we are; if we wish them to assimilate with us in due time. I can think of no more direct method of accomplishing that objective than allowing the boys and girls to go from the reservations into the schools of white

children, so that they can grow up in that environment, thereby^ becoming accustomed to the ways of the whites, and go home to their tepees at night. In this way they would be put in a position to compete and give to the country the kind of service of v hich they are capable.
I could say a great deal more on this matter, Mr. Speaker, but I feel that if I use up any more time I shall probably be depriving other hon. members of the opportunity to give an expression of their feelings in this regard. After all, it is a matter which affects every one of us; it is not a party matter; it is an national matter, a matter of great concern. I shall therefore content myself by saying that I heartily approve this resolution, if it is impossible to have a royal commission. I really believe that it would be better to have a royal commission. Perhaps the establishment of a committee to go into this problem will be the first step leading to the appointment of a royal commission, because the members of this committee, after wrestling with the problem for a year, may become convinced that a royal commission is the only solution and may so recommend. However, let me repeat that since it is impossible to have a royal commission at the present time I heartily approve the appointment of this committee and again wish to congratulate the minister on having introduced the resolution.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
I welcome the introduction of this resolution, Mr. Speaker, by the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen). Some of the Indians have been asking for a royal commission, but if this committee is given sufficient power to
bring before it an adequate representation of Indians, in order to present their grievances, perhaps it will serve the purpose.
Speaking for the Indians of my constituency I would say there are many things that need to be cleaned up. We have young Indians from the Fisher river and Pequis reserves lying in gaol for trapping muskrats. These young Indians still feel they are within their rights, and they do not believe they have done anything wrong. We may be able to straighten out such matters in such a committee. There is also the question of the land in St. Peter's reserve which was leased or sold to the provincial government; that is the Netley marsh. If this land was surrendered, as the government maintains, why do the Indians still claim they never agreed to the sale? That is another matter than can be straightened up in this committee.
The young Indians of the constituency of Selkirk who fought overseas and are now coming back have new ideas. They have seen how other people live. They have been trained in the army, and they question such practices as taking water from a river into which, a little further upstream, the sewage of a town is dumped. These boys have learned that sanitation, hygiene and nutrition are essential to decent living. Tuberculosis is increasing among the Indians. Last year the department granted more money than ever before, but I am quite sure a great deal more will have to be spent before this disease is brought under control. There is the question of old age pensions for Indians; that can be discussed in this committee. There is the matter of the conditions in which some of these old Indians are living in the northern part of my constituency; we can bring that before this committee when the time comes.
There will be educational problems which require to be straightened out. I have in mind as one example the fact that when an Indian becomes enfranchised his children immediately have to stop going to the Indian school, though there may not be a school operated by the provincial government within ten or twenty miles. I am sure the federal Indian department and the provincial department of education could do a good job by cooperating to see that 'these Indians have an opportunity to obtain an education.
Again I welcome the appointment of this committee, which will afford these Indian bands, Indian organizations and people interested in the welfare of the Indians an opportunity to present their views, comments and recommendations to members of the Senate and House of Commons in an endeavour to correct any wrongs that may exist and in gen-

Indian Affairs-Joint Committee
eral to legislate for the improvement of the welfare of our Indians. I do not intend to say any more at this time, since I understand the minister would prefer to have any complaints brought before the committee. I am happy to be on it and am looking forward to the opportunity in the near future of bringing to the attention of the committee the representations of the various Indian bands in the constituency of Selkirk.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
I should like to make two or three brief observations on this lengthy resolution. In the first place I do not see that any good purpose will be served by a lengthy debate, such as seems to be developing at the present time. What is wanted is to get the resolution passed and the committee at work. The Indians themselves are sick and tired, I know from speaking to a large number of them, of people talking over their problems, making observations about them, and getting nothing done. As far as I can see, we are just wasting the time of the house in debating this matter at the present time. Let us pass the resolution and get something done.
As far as I have been able to determine, the majority of the Indians, and certainly a very large number of organizations which are friendly to the Indians and are supporting them, have been pressing for the appointment of a royal commission. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) has gone at some length into the matter of a royal commission and some of the advantages which might accrue from it. Personally I think that would be a better way to handle this investigation into Indian affairs, if for no other reason than I think it would have been more satisfactory to the Indians and those friendly to the Indians than a parliamentary committee of this kind. However, since the government have decided on a parliamentary committee I believe they can be assured that we shall all give full cooperation, as I am sure will be the case with the various organizations interested in the welfare of our Indians.
The minister has indicated that full opportunity will be given the Indians to make representations to this committee, and I trust he used the word "full" in its widest meaning.
I hope there will be no tendency to put pressure on Indians from any reservation to prevent them from bringing forward their problems and making what complaints they have to make. That was one of the reasons why a lot of them wanted a royal commission appointed. They felt that with a parliamentary committee they would have less, chance to be heard and less chance to put forward their 
own points of view. I trust that we shall now go ahead and pass the resolution instead of wasting any more time in talk.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) for bringing forward this resolution. The Indians in my district did not want a royal commission; they wanted the problem dealt with in this manner. They felt that a royal commission would be too cold-blooded an affair; they wanted some body appointed, something in the way of a round-table conference, before which they could place their problems; they wanted to sit down with the members of parliament who make the laws.
I met the brotherhood which represents the Indians on the northwest coast of British Columbia; I also made a visit to the Indian village of Old Massett on the Queen Charlotte islands in order to find out what grievances they had, and they had many. The education of the Canadian Indian in years gone by has not been very good and many new requirements have to be provided for. The whole thing is a disheartening mess. I found in the school at Old Massett that the grade seven pupils were using grade six books while the grade five pupils were using grade four books. They simply did not have proper textbooks for the children. The Indian agent has been told of this but no action has been taken. There are no lights in the school and as hon. members know, in that latitude the days are rather short in the winter time. There is no library; there are no reference books, and no help has been received from the agent in connection with these deficiencies.
The Indians want to know who inspects the school. Apparently there is no proper inspection. The Indians tell me that the boarding schools are under the domination or control of the various religious denominations. They would like to have schools like we have, that is, government controlled education. It is granted that the people running these schools have the highest motives, but too many of them are picked for their religious qualifications rather than for their ability to teach, under modern conditions especially.
The teacher in the school at Old Massett is receiving $95 a month plus the cost of living bonus. I am told that the salaries paid in some of the residential schools are as low as $60 a month. When we realize the conditions a schoolteacher in an Indian village is up against we must know that we cannot get the right class of teacher to teach in an Indian village unless higher salaries are paid. It would pay this country to pay these teachers

Indian Affairs-Joint Committee
more than, is normally paid to the ordinary day schoolteacher. These teachers have more difficult problems to meet and they must be more understanding. If proper salaries were paid a better class of teacher could be induced to go on the Indian reservations and make the teaching of these people their life work.	.
The inspector of the department states that day schools are more effective than residential schools. Apparently the residential schools break up the school day into so many hours of schooling and so many hours of actual work. Under modern conditions such a procedure is outlawed. These people will have to .adapt themselves to present-day technology development at relatively a much faster rate than we had to.
I have here a description of the sanitary conditions in the village of Kitketla. These people state that they have no drinking water, that some people must depend upon rain water. Others dig holes in the ground but they cannot go very deep because of the bedrock. Hon. members know the kind of water you get when you can go down only two or three feet. Is it any wonder that there is so much sickness among the Indians? They tell me that there is a lake up on the hill and that all the government would have to do is to put in a pipe to provide water for the village. The Indian agent promised to have this done this summer, but nothing has happened. Previous Indian agents made no attempt to solve this problem.
The condition of the school is, to put it mildly, a disgrace. It is contended that the school is a source of tuberculosis. There are forty-eight families there and four babies died in three months. The size of the school is thirty-four by twenty-two feet; it has a seating capacity of thirty-six, and seventy pupils are registered. The older ones go in the morning and the younger ones in the afternoon. Some of the children do not want to go to school because the floor is full of holes through which the rats can crawl. This is the condition that these people have to face.
The Indians in British Columbia do not
come under treaty rights. A total of $20,000,000 has been spent on Indians during the past fifty years and this amounts to $4.10 per capita per annum for the Indians in that province. They would like to see some sort of credit set-up arranged so that they could buy their own fishing gear and boats and not be under the control of the canning companies. This would give them a degree of independence which they have not had in years gone by.
Indian Affairs branch will have to take some responsibility for housing conditions in the canneries. No matter what is done on the reservation, when these people go to the canneries the conditions under which they must live are definitely bad for their health. The provincial authorities are not doing a great deal about the matter. The housing situation generally in most villages is bad and I do not think enough money has been spent in providing proper facilities.
I could give more details of the cases that have been laid before me, but now that this committee is to be set up they can be presented by the Indians themselves. I hope that the Indians and organizations such as the brotherhood will have ample opportunities to present their cases and that officialdom from the Indian Affairs branch will not take up too much time. I trust that the Indians will be able to speak their mind about what they want in the way of education and that representatives of the various churches will not be allowed to take up too much of the time of the committee. I know the Indians can make it very plain what they want if they are given the opportunity.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, until the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) spoke I had not intended to speak on this motion. The hon. member for Lethbridge suggested that the Indians should be exempted from military service. That would be an insult to the Indians in my riding. Practically every male Indian in my riding enlisted for overseas service, and many of them never came back.
