subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
I stand corrected. But I do not think the committee should deal with the matter at all. It should be left as is. Let the Indians decide for themselves. They will enlist without any persuasion from any government, as they did in my riding.
The enfranchised Indians should, I believe, have a good deal of consideration from this committee because it is the enfranchised Indians who often find themselves at the parting of the ways, unable to look after themselves after a few years awav from their

Indian Affairs-Joint Committee

tribe. In many cases they cannot even get schooling; they cannot get hospitalization, and township or county often will not give them hospitalization. I know of one Indian boy who developed tuberculosis of the leg, and the hospital and doctors' bills-mostly the hospital-ran to over $3,000. Eventually the county had to pay it. But I believe that is the responsibility of the government. These people are not paying any taxes; they never did pay any tax, and I doubt that they ever will, as they are on government land. These enfranchised Indians should be looked after.
I notice that of late years the Indian Affairs branch has been selling islands and lake shores. This has resulted in closing off many Indians who act as guides for tourists from going ashore in order to cook the noonday meals for those they guide. Upon all lakes and streams where there are Indian lands, proper provision should be made for the Indians for this purpose.
The hon. member who spoke before me mentioned the pay of teachers in the Indian schools. Pay is essential, of course, but the most important thing for the teacher in an Indian school is to have an understanding of the Indian. The teacher must first learn to know the Indians and how to win their confidence. Once they have won the confidence of the Indians they can teach them, but they cannot teach them before having that. I have found that the Indian boys and girls, if given proper teaching, will do as well as if not better than the white boys and girls, as the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) has said. They make wonderful pupils and wonderful citizens of Canada if given half a chance.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my only purpose in participating in this debate is to emphasize the urgency of giving the utmost consideration to the question of nontreaty Indians. During the past few years we have had a bitter experience in our part of the country in connection with two bands of Indians. One of them up until recently was a non-treaty band and the other is still a non-treaty band.
Among these non-treaty Indians we find a roving group of people not limited to any specific area but moving seasonally to engage in various types .of work, perhaps farm work during the harvest and trapping during the winter. The two bands that I am particularly concerned with, the Crees and the Ohippewas of the Rocky Mountain House and White Court districts pose a tremendous problem because of the incidence of disease among them, venereal disease and tuberculosis

particularly. During certain times of the year these Indians come out from the areas they inhabit during the winter and engage in harvest operations among the whites. I contend that this is a menace to the white people of those areas. About two years ago the district health nurse at Rocky Mountain House advised me that if the public were aware of the infant mortality rate among those Indians they would be appalled. A certain doctor responsible for checking these Indians for military service stated that he could not O.K. one of them for military service because of the incidence of both venereal disease and tuberculosis.
I wish to emphasize that during recent times one tribe has agreed to accept treaty. I understand there is an agreement whereby Indians cannot be forced to accept treaty and to establish themselves upon a reservation, but in my opinion where the prevalence of disease among them is such as to jeopardize the general health of all the people, whites and others, in that area, drastic action Aould be taken.
There are no educational facilities for the Indians of the non-treaty bands. There are no hospital facilities at all for them, and as I indicated earlier, the increase in disease among them is staggering.
I could not speak on this subject without paying public tribute to one who has done a tremendous work among these two bands of Indians and who has received very little if any public acclaim for his services. I have in mind one Hem-y Stelfox, the first public game warden in the province of Alberta, one who has given generously of his means and his time on behalf of these Indians and has been refused on more than one occasion repayment of the few paltry dollars he has paid out of his own pocket in order to meet some emergency such as illness among these Indians. Mr. Stelfox, I understand, was upon one occasion offered a position as Indian agent, but the wage offered was much less than he paid to his most poorly paid hired man. To me it seemed an insult. But I wish to emphasize that he is not looking for a position or compensation. I believe that he is deserving of the highest tribute I am capable of paying for the magnificent work that he has done among these Indians. But the work is becoming beyond what any one man can do, and the government must step in and take definite action to clear up a bad situation which has developed, I trust, therefore, that the committee will not overlook the position of the non-treaty Indians and that as a result of committee deliberations their problems will be removed.

Indian Affairs-Joint Committee

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understood from the minister last night that he was hopeful there would be little debate on this resolution and therefore I Shall be brief. We are pleased to see that the government are doing something about the Indians, if it is only the setting up of a committee. About a month ago I placed on the order paper a resolution proposing :
That, in the opinion of this house, the government consider the advisability of setting up a royal commission, which should include Indian representation, to study the whole matter of the treatment of Indians in Canada; the relation of the present Indian Act to its ability to fulfil the treaties signed by these Indians, and to recommend to parliament those changes necessary in the administration of Indian affairs and the Indian Act which will make it possible to properly fulfil the treaty obligations, and to properly provide for the future well-being of the Indians of Canada.
The government, however, has already seen fit to set up this committee, and we support this part of the resolution. I believe that if the committee gets out in the field, discovers the actual conditions, and really does the work required of it, it will have on it hands a job much larger than may be anticipated at this present time. I hope that one of its recommendations will be that such a committee shall become more or less permanent. My reason for this suggestion lies in the very nature of the problem, the fact that we have in this country about 130,000 Indians who, living on reserves or off them, have no way +o air their grievances, no official voice by v' :eh to express approval or disapproval of what is being done, no way of protesting against undesirable conditions. We as Canadian people have a responsibility here to see that these people are properly treated. I am of opinion that the conditions which have been allowed to develop among the Indians with regard to their health, economic situation and training facilities are nothing less than a monument of disgrace to those who have been in power in Canada and have allowed human beings to suffer the conditions which exist among a very large majority of our Indian people.
What the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) has said on this matter is quite true. When the minister is closing the debate he might give us a statement as to what the infant mortality rate is among the Indians; it is reported to be over SO per cent in some areas. We are pleased that this matter of public health improvement has been regarded so seriously that the government has decided to hand the subject over to another department, the Department of National Health and Welfare. I believe that surveys in the 63260-931
northern area and reports have already been made, and I would ask that the report of the committee of medical men who investigated conditions in northern parts of Canada should be made available to this committee, so that we may know something of the magnitude of the problem facing us, and be able to take proper steps to provide adequate medical services to the Indians.
Those young Indians who volunteered to serve in the Canadian army and served abroad have learned a good many things, and what has struck them most forcibly is the method of controlling sanitary conditions and the scientific approach to nutritional problems, matters of which the Indians in general are in complete ignorance. The economic conditions of these people are simply deplorable. They cannot live nobly and well, if they have not the means of proper living; and my experience in visiting them, hearing reports, attending their attempts at holding conventions of one kind and another, both provincial and federal, convinces me that the economic condition constitutes a tremendous and immediate problem. What first drew my attention to this matter was that in my own constituency, although agriculture is supposed to pay pretty well these days, according to a report from one reserve where there are forty-six families, only ten of them are actively engaged in agriculture, that is in raising grain or cattle or both; the other thirty-six have no means of earning a livelihood other than going out to work for the white men in the neighbouring areas, or cutting wood and hauling it to town; and if their ponies are able to haul a fairly large load they may get two or three dollars for it, but in many cases they may get less. It is time we took these matters into account. I hope a careful study will be made as to the basis on which these people can be made self-supporting with an adequate standard of living.
The Indian himself is a good man. There is a lot of inherent goodness among Indians. The Indian creed is "Love and help thy brother", which I think will be admitted to be a fairly high code of ethics, and he lives out his belief. Indians help one another. Moreover, the Indian is a conserver of natural resources. If there are a number of muskrats or beaver, or a herd of reinder, or whatever the Indian makes his livelihood from, in any area, he realizes that enough should be left each year in order to propagate those animals or provide that fur or that food, and he always leaves a sufficient number there. In this respect the Indian is more scientific than the white man, with all his cunning. Too often the white trapper will move in on
Indian Affairs-Joint Committee

Indian trapping grounds and take the whole cache, clean out the whole area, so that in many cases the Indians have to move away or remain without the means of livelihood. One of the best things the Indian Affairs branch has done has been to carry out its programme of fur farming, and I hope that this committee in its recommendations will advocate the continuation and expansion of that programme.
The Indian is suspicious of white men. I think this is largely because he has been fooled so often, and because fur trading companies operating in the north robbed the Indians of their livelihood. They took their furs and paid the Indians practically nothing for them. They are the people to whom the Indians must go for provisions, for food, for ammunition, for most of their supplies. The exploitation which we used to read about as having occurred in the early days in Canada is still being carried on in the northern areas of this country as far as the Indian is concerned.
Treaty rights is one of the matters for consideration by this committee. I am pleased to notice that, because although it is a difficult and involved question it is also an important one. You will find that the Indians still have copies of old treaties made between themselves and early French governors who came to this countiy long before Canada became part of the British empire. You will find treaties made with representatives of the British people who conquered Canada, and between representatives of Great Britain and Indians who fought for the English at the time of the American war of independence and came to Canada to the Six Nations reserve. You will find treaties made with governors throughout Ontario and further west. It will be difficult to see to it that the Indian Act and the administration of the act fulfil all the obligations made under the various treaties. In the west, treaties were made somewhat later, after the northwest rebellion. Promises were made by the representatives of the queen. The Indians, in reading over those treaties, find that they have been broken, that, for example, it was carefully and deliberately provided that day schools should be established on each reserve, but that no such day schools have been provided. Other understandings in connection with the treaties were arrived at in conversations between Indians and officials of the government. For example, the Indians say they made it clear that they did not want their children to be taken outside Canada and forced to fight the battles of the white man

outside the country. Officials of the government at that time said, "No; we want you to live at peace among yourselves and with your white brothers and you will not be called upon to fight the wars of the queen outside Canada." But the present government instituted conscription and conscripted Indians off the reserves right in the province of Saskatchewan. These Indians had not volunteered; they had been promised these rights by treaty, and therefore they said, "You are breaking your treaty with us". What could they do? Could they go and complain to the Indian agent? Well, the agent would write to the department and ask for a directive and he would be told in reply that he should encourage the Indians to join.
When you break your word with an Indian he remembers it and it is no wonder the Indians are suspicious of their white brothers. Very often portions of reserves set aside for Indians have been sold to municipalities or to settlers and the Indian on the reserve wonders what has happened to the money he was supposed to get. He has no accounting. He has no way of saying, "You sold this land for so much money; where is that money?" He says, "By what right did you sell it? You set aside this land for us; you did so by treaty, and now you sell some of it." Well, they are told that they agreed to this; but who agreed to it? There is no record of anyone agreeing to it. The Indians understand that money was set aside in trust for them, but there is no accounting of the trust fund and they want an accounting. They want to know where the money is; they want to know something about the interest. What was done with it? The answer is, "It was used to pay you so much a year in treaty money; then there is the maintenance of the aged and the sick, and we have done many other things for you."
In the days when there was i)o crop in western Canada the Indians did not get relief from the municipalities. Quite often they had to pay for their own relief out of their trust fund and they lived at a terrifically low standard, as they do now. When there are only ten. families on a small reserve and the only means of livelihood is farming, the living conditions of these people are such that they cannot be healthy. They cannot assimilate education; they cannot improve their conditions, and they are powerless to speak. They have no means of redress.
The fight of the Indian to-day is a fight against ignorance, against poverty, against fear; and it will be a fight for democracy.
I am sorry that this committee will not have some group representing the Indians. I am sorry that it will not have some means

Inaian Affairs-Joint Committee
of such representation, somebody who can sit in on the deliberations, or persons chosen from selected groups in various parts of Canada.
I should like to see an Indian from the Mic-macs of the maritimes. I should like to see one from the Iroquois reserve and one from the Caughnawaga. I should like to see on the committee representatives who can listen to the deliberations, and I would recommend to the government that a place be made on the committee for representative groups of Indians from across Canada.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext: It might not be a peaceable committee.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext: A good thing every now and then is a good fight. I believe we would avoid a good many mistakes.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext: I am a peaceable man; I agree with you.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
I appreciate the hon. gentleman's qualities. If this suggestion were adopted, then for the first time in the history of the country, in the making of important legislation, the Indians would at least have a voice. They would have representatives chosen by the people themselves and that would help to prevent mistakes, because . I do not believe that we understand entirely the position of the Indians. There are good men on the Indian reserves, man of ability, with qualities of leadership.
I should like to see representation from Manitoba. There was a young Indian from Manitoba on the committee who interviewed the minister recently and I had the honour of listening to him. He had volunteered from that province. He could not pass the medical examination to start with, but after medical treatment, special training and settingup exercises, he turned out to be a man of fine physique, a man of courage, and he won the Military Medal. He belonged to the paratroopers and went behind the enemy's lines in Sicily and Italy. He could tell the committee a few things.
I should like to see representation from Saskatchewan, from the Sioux, the Cree, the Blackfeet and the Stony Indians. They could tell us something about their treatment. We also need representation from British Columbia, where I understand no treaties at all were made with the Indians. They have no means of making themselves heard. They cannot say, "Here are our treaties and you are breaking them." Under proper representation, however, those Indians could put their views before the committee. I would earnestly suggest that representatives of these Indians sit in with the committee throughout the whole of its deliberations.
I would also direct the attention of the government to education and a training programme for the Indians. Evidence is abundant to prove that of the few Indians, out of the whole 125,000 or 130,000 who get an opportunity for education, so many have gone so far and done so much, that proof is hardly necessary for my contention that the Indian could be made into a great man and a great leader. Under existing educational and training facilities, however, the opportunities are small.
Here is a school statement from the department's own report of 1945 showing that out of the whole of the Indians of Canada in every province and in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, some 132,000 Indians, the children from the ages of seven to sixteen who went to school in 1945, only 56 reached grade nine, 171 reached grade eight, 400 reached grade seven and 600 reached grade six. Of thousands of Indian children, that is the extent of their education.
These people can never advance until that condition is changed. I agree that it is not an easy problem but it is one that must be approached with understanding. It must be approached scientifically and with a view to providing efficient training and education for the Indians. They must be established in decent homes. It is no use having children coming to school if they are to spread disease among the others. They cannot come from homes where there is filth or dirt, because in that case they will only spread these diseases. They must be established economically and schools must be provided where the children will have an opportunity for proper education which will develop their abilities.
The present system of residential schools is not meeting the problem. I know there are residential schools where good work is done but there are many where children are not getting an opportunity of attending classes. Moreover, they attend classes for half a day. Actually the number of hours spent in the classroom is not sufficient for the number of students who show ability to carry on and to take on further training.
I am going to recommend for the study of this committee-and I hope it will be available to it-a complete report of what has been done in the United States with regard to freeing these people, giving them power and raising them from the status of wards to the position of free men.
Citizenship is a matter of contention. There are many Indians who want it and many who do not. I hope that this committee will thresh it out. My contention is that since these Indians show capacity and a desire to become citizens they should be given citizenship rights;

Indian Affairs-Joint Committee
and if they so desire they should also retain their rights under the treaty, as is done in the United States. No citizenship should ever be forced upon these people if they do not want it.
If this committee finds, when it starts its work, that it requires so much attention that it will have to be continued as a committee I hope that it will be set up year after year to receive reports from the Indians until the day comes when they can speak for themselves.

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext: The hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) made one statement which should be corrected at once. As I understood him, he said that the infant mortality rate for Indians was, he understood, 50 per cent.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext: I should like to correct that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext: On reflection I am sure he would like to correct it.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
I have not all the figures and reports, but from the reports that I have for certain areas in northern parts of Canada the infant mortality rate is 50 per cent.
_ Mr. CLAXTON: Fifty per cent? Of course it is possible that at a locality two children may be born and one of them die within a year of the birth of the two of them, and that would make the rate 50 per cent in that spot. It would give a totally wrong impression to say that the rate for Indians is 50 per cent or anything like it. The rate, of course, is very much less. I have the rate for deaths from diseases peculiar to the first year of life. This is the infant mortality rate measured per 100,000. While the rate for Indians undoubtedly is higher than the rate for white people, it is quite different from anything like 50 per cent.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext: Has the minister the comparative figures for the whites?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext: I believe we can give this information morq suitably when the committee sits. I should not like to take up the time now when there is a strong desire on the part of all hon. members to have this resolution carried and the committee set up and at work.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
Is the minister sure that the rate is estimated on the 100,000? Is not the infant mortality rate considered as so many per thousand live births?
Mr. CLAXTONc It could be either way:
I am giving it as it was given to me. The health of Indians has been a matter of serious concern to the government for some time. On

November 1, 1945, as the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) said, responsibility for the health and hospitalization of Indians was transferred to the Department of National Health and Welfare.
At the time of the transfer the Department of Mines and Resources, Indian Affairs branch, had prepared plans for a considerable extension of hospital and health facilities among the Indians and Eskimos. Since we have had the responsibility in the other department we have reviewed these plans and extended them in some respects. If hon. members will look at the estimates they will see that there is a considerable increase in the amount provided over last year. I hope that this is an increase for which we shall have the support of members in every part of the house.
With regard to the health of Eskimos in the far north I may say that we had a conference here on February 8 of this year, which was attended by some of the prominent doctors who have made the trip to the far north in recent years, such doctors as Doctor Dennis Jordan, Doctor Campbell Laidlaw, Doctor George S. McCarthy, Doctor George Hooper, and Doctor W. L. Crewson representing the National Institute for the Blind. We have had their assistance in drawing up plans for dealing with the exceedingly difficult problems of the Eskimo, and we hope to be able to do something further to extend the service that they have already been given in that field where there are some 7,700 Eskimos scattered over a territory of nearly 700,000 square miles.
The hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) spoke about the possibility of a hospital being constructed on the shores of James bay. That is under consideration. There are some 3,759 Indians in the neigbour-hood, plus some 1,200 Eskimos on the eastern shores of James bay and Hudson bay. It is felt that a hospital or additional facilities are needed there, and that is receiving consideration.
Consideration is being given; indeed active steps are being taken to increase hospital accommodation in many centres. Only on Wednesday of last week I visited the band of the Six Nations at or near Brantford which was referred to by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). There I saw the Lady Willingdon hospital, a small hospital of eighteen beds, with two doctors and three nurses, which is doing excellent work in looking after the health of the Six Nations Indians on the Six Nations reserve. So far as the statistics go I think it will be found that the health of the Indians on that reserve is probably as good as that of the white people

Indian Affairs-Joint Committee
around in every respect except-that of tuber-culois, where the death-rate is considerably higher.
The suggestions that have been made by hon. members in a helpful way during the course of this debate with regard to the health and hospitalization of Indians will be taken into consideration. When the committee sits we shall have available any information that we have, and we shall be prepared to discuss any matters of interest to the members of the committee or in the interests of the welfare of the Indians themselves.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext: In reply to the minister I should like to say my plea was for this committee to get the actual statistics with regard to the health of Indians, and to clear up the doubts. When I made my statement I was not referring to the infant mortality rate as 50 per cent, but that report had been brought down.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
I also wish to Join with others in expressing a word of commendation to the minister for having introduced this motion to-day. I should also like to congratulate him on the splendid presentation that he made.
It is quite true that I am not the chief of an Indian clan; I am too young, but I hope I can lay claim to the fact that I have been, am now and hope I always shall be, a friend of the Indian. He is not of the mentality of the white man; but I believe the constitution of this committee offers a splendid opportunity to do something worth while for the elevation of that part of our human race.
In the constituency that I represent there are two residential schools, one at Elkhorn, Manitoba, of which I have heard splendid reports, but I am not so intimately familiar with the work done in that school as I am with the work done in another school a couple of miles from Brandon. For the last thirty-five years I have been in close touch with the work of that school, first under the direction of the late Doctor Ferrier, than under Doctor Doyle, now retired, who succeeded him, and at the present time under the Reverend 0. B. Stroppe, who has a long experience in Indian affairs. I can bear testimony to the splendid work which has been done in that school down through the years. Those who have attended that school have, in later life, gone on to other seats of learning and have made their mark, not only educationally but in whatever vocation they followed, agriculture or otherwise.
I have heard it said frequently, that after finishing their courses at the residental schools
very often those young boys and girls go back to the reserves and lapse right back into the old ways. I have made inquiry in that connection, and I find that in many instances they do lapse for perhaps a year or two but that almost invariably they stage a comeback, so that a little- later you find them taking a more forward place in the affairs of the band and endeavouring to make a better livelihood than otherwise would have been the case. I believe a great deal depends upon the teacher. This matter was mentioned by the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser). We can quite appreciate how difficult it must be for those in charge of the educational section of the department to secure and retain really good teachers on many reserves. Like the rest of us, teachers are human, and probably the conditions they find in regard to residence for white people on the reserves are not of the best, so that I believe this subject must be a headache for those in the department having charge of education.
In the western part of my constituency we have a reserve to which I should like to take the minister some day, when the crops are flourishing, to show him what has been done there from an agricultural point of view. We have there an efficient farm instructor, and the progress in agriculture that has been made on that reserve is to my mind, simply marvellous. It is good land; they raise good crops; they till the soil well, and they have made a marked success during the past few years. Apparently those Indians have a new spirit to-day. They have fine herds of stock; they are not pure bred, but I believe the day is coming when those young Indians will be exhibiting at the fairs, and you will see them carrying off some of the red ribbons.
Again, we must not forget the loyalty of the Indians, many of whom have served their country. The Indian has always been loyal to the best of his ability. I recall a sentence or two written by Lord Dufferin after he made an extended trip across Canada during his regime as governor general. After speaking of the attitude of the average Indian toward our sovereign, he went on to speak of the-
. . . untutored halfbreed hoisting some cloth or rag above his humble shanty, and of the stolid Indian in forest or reserve marshaling forth his picturesque symbol of fidelity in glad allegiance to his country's queen.
The Indian has always been loyal, and we would not be loyal to the best traditions of our race if we did not see to it that he is

Indian Affairs-Joint Committee
taken care of and that his living conditions are made better than they have been in the past.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO ACT AND INDIAN ADMINISTRATION GENERALLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to hear so many expressions of appreciation of the fine qualities and characteristics of the Indians. If we really believe what we have said we are all set to give them the advantages that will bring out and develop these qualities, and allow the Indians to make a fine contribution to Canadian life. I thought the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Campbell) performed a useful service in making a survey of Indians who had succeeded in various lines, but I was sorry to learn that three of them had gone to Detroit, one to Ohio and another to New Zealand. More than half of those who have made outstanding successes have left Canada. I believe we should see if we cannot offer them some inducement to serve their own people here. With the advantages they have gained through their experience outside this country they might be the better qualified to come back and help meet the problem here. I believe that would be particularly true of the person who has gone to New Zealand, because when I was in that country a few years ago I was astonished to learn that the Maori people there elect four Maori members to sit in the New Zealand parliament with all the rights of members, including one with the statutory right to be a member of the cabinet. Sometimes that person holds a portfolio; at other times he is a member without portfolio, but they tell you there that one of the best ministers of health they ever had was a Maori. They tell you also that it is not uncommon to have a Maori New Zealander say to a white New Zealander, "Remember the day when my grandfather ate your grandfather," because when the white people went to New Zealand the Maoris were cannibals. So that I think we should learn from other parts of the commonwealth what may be done to develop the possibilities inherent in native peoples.
I hope the minister will not consider that in citing examples of what happens in other places we are being critical. Far too often, it seems to me, the government go on the defensive and try to prove that we are traitors or something of the kind when we mention the possibilities that other countries have explored. I hope they will be good enough to asume that we, too, are ambitious for the record of Canada. We too would like to be proud of our treatment of our native people; and whether we sit on this side or 
the other side we would like to see reforms carried out that will make us the envy of other parts of the commonwealth.
I have only another moment or two at my disposal, Mr. Speaker, but I wish to say that I believe we should give special training to teachers engaged in handling Indian children, and special, training to the administrators who apply the Indian Act. First of all, I believe these persons should be humanists, with social vision and broad sympathies. In my experience, which has been limited, in talking with Indian agents and Indian doctors, too often I have been discouraged by the attitude of these people who have the lives Of the Indians in their hands. Too often they regard the Indians very lightly, with nothing but contempt. I hope that is not a sample of the sort of people who work for the government, and to-day I was glad1 to hear reference made to persons of outstanding accomplishments and achievements in that department.

Motion agreed to.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-OUT-OF-WORK. BENEFITS FOR EX-SERVICE PERSONNEL

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-OUT-OF-WORK. BENEFITS FOR EX-SERVICE PERSONNEL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour which is based upon two telegrams I received this morning, one from the mayor of the town of Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, and the other from the president of the Cape Breton labour council. I have sent copies of the telegrams to the minister so that he knows their subject-matter. Has the government considered the advisability of extending the period for which unemployment insurance benefits may be paid in areas where there is a serious unemployment problem with no immediate relief in sight? Second, has the government considered the advisability of extending the time period for which out-of-work benefits may be paid to ex-service personnel when employment cannot be had in the communities in which they reside?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-OUT-OF-WORK. BENEFITS FOR EX-SERVICE PERSONNEL
speechtext:
The hon. member was good
enough to give me a notice of his question and I may say that I received similar telegrams. I should like to say this for the

Labour Conditions
general information of hon. members. There are 1,106 applicants for work registered at the Glace Bay employment office. Of this number 262 males are receiving unemployment insurance benefits, and 566 veterans' out-of-work benefits. An additional 350 were receiving unemployment insurance benefits, but the period for which they were entitled to these benefits has lapsed and payments have been stopped.
The employment situation on Cape Breton island, including Glace Bay, is not good. It is true that agricultural workers, some men for the coal mines at Sydney and a number for fishing are still required. However, it is not feasible for all those registered for employment to accept the work available and many of them are not able to do the work. Housing, the type of work to be done and the physical disabilities of the unemployed are factors.
The labour department has provided for issuance of transportation to other parts of the country and men are being moved to places where jobs are open, but the general situation in the maritimes is such that possibilities for transfer are not great. Nevertheless, transportation is being supplied where a satisfactory transfer can be arranged. The movement of a number of men from Cape Breton island to the state of Maine for lumbering and logging is being considered. The United States authorities have asked that some men be furnished for this work. It is anticipated that some wharf construction work can proceed early in June and that the repair work in the Sydney shipyards will increase from now on. The situation is under constant study by the labour department and the reconstruction department and everything possible is being done to work out a satisfactory solution.
One of the proposals which was before the dominion-provincial conference was that the dominion government establish a system of assistance to able-bodied unemployed persons. However, pending the conclusion of a general agreement between the dominion and the provinces the responsibility {or such relief is on the local authorities, the municipalities in the first instance, and then the provinces.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO CALLING OP CONFERENCE TO CONSIBER INDUSTRIAL SITUATION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO CALLING OP CONFERENCE TO CONSIBER INDUSTRIAL SITUATION
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the acting leader of the government. In view of disturbing reports of the possibilities of impending industrial strife, has the government considered the advisability of calling a conference of representatives of the government, labour, farmers and employers in an effort to prevent grave economic dislocations?

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO CALLING OP CONFERENCE TO CONSIBER INDUSTRIAL SITUATION
speechtext:
I am not a great believer in having too many conferences, although sometimes they are necessary. Probably my hon. friend has a vivid recollection of the conference called by President Truman. That conference did not do a great deal to increase industrial stability in the United States; at least I do not think so. As I have said before, we have ample machinery for meeting any industrial condition that arises. There are many statements made in the press to-day *which in my judgment show an utter lack of responsibility. Irrespective of the government that may be in power, whether it is made up of my hon. friend's followers or of the official opposition, when you have built up machinery which in a general way is equal to handling these problems, I think it is the duty of employers' organizations and of labour organizations to avail themselves of that machinery. That machinery was created by agreement, in a broad way of course, between the federal government, the provincial government, labour organizations and employers' organizations.
As I said last week in this house, I do not think anyone is rendering a service to his country when he says he will not use the machinery that has been established. subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the vote is taken on the amendment I should like to take a few moments of the committee's time to present the view of the group which I represent with respect to the proposed amendment of the hon. member for Lake Centre.
During the debate which has taken place, particularly between the hon. member for Lake Centre and the Minister of Justice and the Secretary of State, I listened most carefully hoping to get the answers to two questions that arose in my mind. It is those two questions that I should like to discuss briefly before the committee to-night. The first of these is, do we now need a new charter of liberties?
It is sometimes argued, indeed I heard it argued in this very chamber, that we already have Magna Charta, the Petition of Rights, habeas corpus and the Bill of Rights as the root and core of the common law part of the Canadian constitution; that they constitute a sufficient bill of rights to safeguard the liberty of Canadian citizens, and that, therefore, we need no further bill of rights. This argument raises interesting questions particularly in the mind of any person who is familiar with the history of Great Britain, from whom we obtained the common law which is part of the constitution of Canada. These are some of the questions.
Why was it that the British people found it necessary to enact habeas corpus when they already had Magna Charta? And why the Bill of Rights when they already had Magna Charta, the Petition of Right and habeas corpus? I submit that a study of British liberties reveals the fact that they were won gradually and as a result of struggles that lasted over a long period of time. Each charter was a reenactment of charters of freedom previously in existence, together with a statement of expanded liberty, freedoms newly won. Thus the Petition of Right of 1628 reaffirmed the promises of Magna Charta, and in addition to that provided protection for the subjects in Great Britain from the depredations and the encroachments of Charles I.
Again, I submit that habeas corpus in 1679 grew out of article 39 of Magna Charta and was a restatement of Magna Charta and an enlargement upon it. The Bill of Rights of 1689 began by reciting the declaration of rights, which was nothing but a statement of all the individual freedoms which had been won up to that time. Then it went on to declare further freedoms as inviolable for the future protection of the citizens of Britain.
Thus, freedom grew naturally. Each new step was a natural outgrowth of something already in existence. Each new charter was a restatement of and an enlargement upon charters previously granted by the monarch of the time.
That has been the outstanding characteristic of Anglo-Saxon development, and that also, I submit, should be the natural growth of things Canadian. At no time did Britons ever cut themselves off from the past, and I submit that at no time should Canadians ever cut themselves off wholly from things past. But as we grow, it seems to me our enlargement and development should be out of things already in existence.
It is noteworthy that periodically Britons felt that they had to reaffirm the freedoms already won. These reaffirmations always came at a time following great struggles during which miguided monarchs had succeeded in encroachments upon the liberties of the people, or following periods when some freedoms of the people were suspended for the purpose of meeting crises.
We have just emerged from the greatest struggle which the human race has ever faced -sixteen years of it. I say sixteen years of it because we have had two great wars following one another very closely, one economic, and the other military, both the most tragic in all history. In the course of these struggles personal liberties have gradually declined and the powers of the state have correspondingly increased. During both great struggles of those sixteen years we have had a marked but steady and certain decline in human values, and a steady but sure increase in the materialistic emphasis. During the thirties men, women and children starved or were driven half-starved from place to place in their efforts to find food and comfort, and they were hardly noticed by those who were in a position to do something about the matter. In the military war human beings were counted pretty cheap and there was a growing indifference on all sides and in every nation to human suffering and to mass human destruction. I submit that such a decline in the morality of nations and of their estimate of human values undoubtedly does call-for a new bill of rights, a new charter of freedoms of the citizen to meet the conditions of this day.
Churchill and Roosevelt must have felt this need when they declared the Atlantic charter. Unfortunately, the Atlantic charter has not been taken up by the nations. Rather, I submit, it has been forgotten if not tacitly revoked.
Again, during the war we in Canada surrendered to the government some of our free-
Canadian Citizenship

doms in order to help Canada to meet the great crisis which faced us and successfully to achieve our part in the world struggle. I need hardly remind hon. members that we fought that war to preserve our freedoms. Now that the war is over, there is definite need to redefine in clear and unmistakable terms just what freedoms and rights individuals shall have in this country, now and for the future, and just what rights are to be yielded up by the government that have been temporarily surrendered to them by individual Canadians. Governments have a habit of trying to make themselves into the all-powerful "State", and that is something we do not want in Canada. This is the time for the people of this and of every other country to assert their determination not only to preserve freedoms which have been won for them at great cost in the past, but also to enlarge their freedoms, to show their determination to enlarge those freedoms. It seems to me that we must add to the freedoms already won through past generations, and now issue a new declaration of freedoms: freedom of our people to consume what they require of the abundance that we can produce; freedom of choice, which goes hand in hand and closely with the freedom to own property and to conduct a business so long as in the holding of property and the conducting of the business, our citizens do not interfere with the same rights of other citizens in this country; freedoms, I mean, in addition to all freedoms which we have won in the past. I believe, therefore, that- a new charter of liberties of Canadian citizens should now be laid down.
The second question I had in my mind was this: is the amendment presented by the hon. member for Lake Centre the type of restatement of liberties of the subject or the citizen that we want? In the first place, I must say that I do not like to see such an important thing tucked away in an inconspicuous place in a bill such as the citizenship bill, although if it is to be related to a bill at all I can see that this is, perhaps, the best one to which to relate it. However, I should like to urge upon the members of this house the necessity of introducing at the earliest possible time a completely new bill which will be a real charter of Canadian liberties.
There is at least one government in Canada which has already recognized the necessity for such a thing, and I make brief reference to one such measure which has been laid down here in the dominion. I refer to bill 76, passed unanimously by the legislature of Alberta, which is known as "An act respecting the rights of Alberta citizens". I wish to quote two or three sections from it to indicate

exactly what I mean by an enlargement upon freedoms already won. From part I of the bill I first quote sections 3 and 4:
3.	It is hereby declared that every Citizen of Alberta shall be free to hold and cherish his own religious convictions and to worship in accordance with the dictates of his own conscience.
4.	It is hereby declared that every citizen of Alberta shall be entitled to enjoy freedom of expression provided that he does not violate the defamation laws in force in the province or the criminal code of Canada.
5.	It is hereby declared that every citizen of Alberta shall be free in association with other citizens, to assemble for any lawful purpose in accordance with the laws in force in the province.
6.	It is hereby declared that every citizen of Alberta shall be free to engage in the work of his choice which may be available to him within the province.
That is a statement of something which has not been included in any charter in this or any other country, and it is, I submit, an important freedom if people are to be in congenial employment. Next:
7.	It is hereby declared that every citizen of Alberta shall be free to acquire land and enjoy the use of his home and property without interference or molestation, so long as he conforms to the laws in force in the province for safeguarding the lives, property and personal rights of other citizens.
8.	It is hereby declared that every citizen of Alberta shall be free to do or refuse to do any act or thing within the limitations of the laws in force in the province, provided that thereby he does not infringe upon the same right of any other citizen.
I emphasize, Mr. Chairmaa, that that is one of the great freedoms for which the people of the world have fought; freedom of choice, without which there cannot be complete freedom of conscience; and I say that it is most important to have that laid down now in a declaration.
9.	It is hereby declared that every citizen of Alberta of not less than nineteen years of age and not more than sixty years of age is entitled as a right of citizenship to,-
(a)	the opportunity to engage in gainful employment; or	_
(b)	if gainful employment is not available, to a social security pension.
That is, the right of the citizen to consume of the abundance which we produce, even if he has not the opportunity to labour.
These comprise at least some suggestion of the type of bill which might be brought into this House of Commons; and if the hon. member for Lake Centre, or anyone else for that matter, will bring in a bill of that type, a complete declaration of the rights of Canadians citizens, he certainly will have my support. If there is no prospect that a bill of that kind will be brought in and have a good chance to pass this house, naturally I am

Canadian Citizenship
bound to take the next best choice, which is to support the hon. member for Lake Centre in the amendment which he has proposed. But I really believe that it belittles such an important matter as a charter of freedoms and of the rights of individual citizens to have it tucked away in an inconspicuous place in a bill such as we have before us.
Finally, I wish to say this. The rights of citizens have been obscured through sixteen years of conflict, economic and military. And in discussions, political, economic and constitutional, which have taken place between the provinces and the dominion in their attempt to find a satisfactory allocation of the powers of government, we have completely overlooked the most important responsibility we have-the individual citizen of this country. He it is who should be considered; he is the man whose rights should be the fount and source of all the things we do. It is not for us to fight and bicker over what this government or that government shall have the power to do. It is for us to determine and define once again the rights and liberties of our people. Because the rights of our citizens have been obscured, I say it is high time that we clarified the whole situation. I am anxious for that clarification, and I suggest to the hon. member for Lake Centre or to anyone else that if he can see his way clear to bring in a bill of rights of Canadian citizens he will get the enthusiastic support of the group I represent.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext:
With reference to the amendment, I think the time has come for some positive action on the part of the government pertaining to a bill of rights. At this stage there is not much that can be said that has not already been said. I do not know whether this amendment in its present form will answer the purpose; I rather doubt it. I do not know whether it is wise at this stage to add another clause to the citizenship bill, nor do I think it wise to add a preamble. But I feel that a clear and concise statement on the matter of citizenship rights is long overdue, and I think this is a good time for us to consider a bill of rights which will act as a bulwark for the cause of free men.
In the past we have held the theory that the personal liberty of the subject has been fully protected by the British common law and by the Canadian constitution, but now we must face up to realities and realize that the liberty of the subject is not fully protected. I wish to prick the conscience of the committee for a few moments by recalling some episodes to hon. members.
I can well recall the padlock law, which was an abridgement of the right of assembly, and
which is still a part of the law of one of the provinces. I remember well section 98 of the criminal code, which was an assault on the civil liberties of every individual in this country. It took years and years before we were able to get rid of it. I remember also references in this house to various deportations that took place at one time or another in Canada when men were arrested, whisked away, and before legal process could be put into force were taken out of the country.
Most members will recall vividly that the Japs in this country were deprived of both their natural and their legal rights, and I have not much to say about the most recent spy case, except to remark that it was an arbitrary use of government power.
These are not isolated cases. The other day I came across a case which I think will be interesting to the committee. It was reported in the Toronto Telegram of November 10 and reads:
When customers of the Runnymede hardware store complained that they did not like being waited on by a Jew, Earl Fleming, the proprietor, discharged Joseph Moses, twenty-nine year old war veteran, and set off a spontaneous storm of protest from the Canadian Legion . . . Earle Burgess, of St. Thomas, president of the Canadian Legion's Ontario command, labelled such discrimination "a vicious thing which must be crushed by all right-thinking Canadians."
I bring this to the attention of the committee because we find here a man who was fit to fight but not fit to serve. The Toronto Star of that day carried an editorial in which it said:
It is a disgraceful thing that a veteran, or anyone else for that matter, should lose his job in a Toronto hardware store because the customers "did not like being waited on by a Jew." The man in question was educated in the schools of the district in -which he recently found employment after returning from service in France. He -was good enough to serve his country overseas, but not good enough, it seems, to wait upon his fellow citizens when they were buying hardware. Those who complained about him and lost him his position should be ashamed of their narrowness and prejudice. They have the consolation of knowing that their attitude is exactly that which Hitler approved and practised.
The Toronto Globe and Mail, which haa always put up a good fight for civil liberties, had this to say:
There are no words of condemnation too harsh to apply to the people in the neighbourhood of Runnymede store, who took it upon themselves to protest the employment of a Jewish war veteran as a clerk in the store. Complaint was not based upon discourtesy or inefficiency, which might have been a legitimate reason for objection, but simply because the young man was a Jew. It is a disgrace to the whole community that such barefaced prejudice should exhibit itself in this manner. It is the negation of everything that the word British should convey.
Canadian Citizenship

Further down.
The least favourable aspect of this matter is that these prejudice-ridden people were depriving of his job a young man who had willingly risked his life in their defence, in the armed forces of the country. He was in the army for three years, and saw active service in Europe. As he has justly said, no one told him he wasn't good enough to serve on account of his religion. All too little credit has been given to the Jewish people in Canada for the extent of their war effort, for that matter. On the most conservative estimates, not counting those who may have served in other allied forces, no fewer than 10,116 Canadian Jews served in the army, 5,870 in the air force, and 573 in the navy.' These comprise ten per cent of the Jewish population, a most admirable record. Of the 800 casualties, more than 200 made the supreme sacrifice. More than 165 won decorations.
Again:
In the light of all this, it might be asked when some Canadians are going to become mature. Those who criticize or display prejudice against any racial or religious group are vulgarians. They are consumed with an envy for obvious talent, or resent the willing capacity for hard work. It is time they put aside such unworthy attitudes and agree to live and let live. Because certain mean people vented their evil spite upon a man whose only crime was a difference in religion and ancestry, the whole community is a meaner place in which to live. It is time these displays of prejudice were stopped.
I would point out that the name of this hardware store was the Runnymede-a historic name indeed; for it was at Runnymede that the first blow for freedom was struck. I put this to the committee: Who understood better the lesson of Runnymede, the soldier who was deprived of his job or the people who had complained?
I pass on to my next point, which is this. Our people need education in citizenship. It is important that the laws be codified and be added to, and it is important also that we put upon our statute books a bill of rights in order to protect people not only against other individuals but against governments, yes, against governments which are sometimes colourblind.
It is often necessary to restate principles that appear only too obvious. I know the argument used is that if you write a law you narrow it, but it is better to make it too narrow than to have it entirely neglected. I do not think the present amendment covers the ground. I do not think the mover felt that in forty-four words he can write a bill of rights, although I should compliment him on the words he carefully used. We should serve notice upon this House of Commons and upon those who are responsible, that the battle is on; that the members from all sides of the house have just started to fight; that the forces are now deployed; that we do not intend to give up at the present time, and that the gov-

eminent is now notified that we intend that it shall in due time produce a bill of rights which will be acceptable not only to the members of the house but also to the country at large.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext:
Before the hon. member for Lake Centre speaks I wish to say a few words. Most hon. members would be favourable to a bill of rights that would outline adequately, or as adequately as we can, the rights of the Canadian citizen. I believe the hon. member for Lake Centre would be the last person to say that, his amendment has done that. He has made an attempt to do that, but I believe that no sooner had he written it than he realized its shortcomings.
One thing of which I am sure, is that a bill of rights should not be made a part of a section of this bill. If a bill of rights is to be put into this bill at all it should go in as a preamble, and then it would become a guide to those who must interpret the citizenship act. But I wish to say something tht has not been said in the long debate on this amendment, namely, that no matter how broad and comprehensive a bill of rights may be it will not protect the rights of the citizens of Canada unless there is the will to protect them.
Mention has been made of the fact that in the United States they have a bill of rights written into the constitution, but it does not mean that every citizen in the United States is assured of his rights within the constitution. Those of us who have been close to affairs during the last thirty or more years realize that, despite the United States bill of rights, in that country things have been done to its citizens that would make any citizen of any country blush with shame. What happened during the war of 1914-18? As a matter of fact there were very little rights that any one had in the United States. Undoubtedly things have improved in the last few years. We hope that they will go on improving because there is still need to extend and broaden the rights of the negro in the United States, and he is a citizen. Therefore I would say that unless we in Canada have the will to protect essential rights, regardless of what we have in this bill or in the constitution, those rights will not be protected.
I do not believe that we can go so far as to say there can never be any interference with a citizen's rights that we would put in a bill. The time may come in the life of a country when, for the preservation of its life, it must, like an individual, take action which may at times seem to us arbitrary and cruel. But the times in which this action must be taken

Canadian Citizenship
should be very few, and the people should always be on the alert to see that the government does not go too far.
We remember that, after the fall of France, thousands of people who had come into Great Britain as refugees and who had been extended the protection of the British government and the constitution were swept up all at once and interned. The authorities considered that this action was necessary at that time because the preservation of the state itself was the most important thing that faced the people. But that did not continue very long. As soon as conditions became a little more stable they began sifting out the good from the bad and getting back to normal. Some of them came over here. They sent a representative over here, and those of us who heard him speak before the defence of Canada regulations committee really got an earful of how the British people respected the rights of individuals, excepting in moments of great peril.

Yes, that was the name. The hon. member for Spadina said that we need education in citizenship. We need education in more than that; we need education in tolerance and in human rights. Once we depart from dealing with man as man, there is nothing to indicate where we are to stop. It is a well known fact that Hitler began with the persecution of the Jews, but he ended up by depriving everybody in Germany of liberty. We have come pretty close to that in Canada. Until we get away from that and consider the rights of every human individual we are not going to protect those rights as they should be protected.
The principle of the amendment is something that I would support, but the amendment itself is so restricted in its terms that I do not see there is anything to be accomplished by adding it to the bill.

To a large degree I
agree with the hon. member who has just spoken. His remarks were like a breath of fresh air in this debate. I believe in the British way of doing things. We have heard a lot this evening and in previous days on this debate about the bill of rights. What we need to-day is a bill of responsibilities. This evening I was asked a question by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar with respect to certain conditions in this country. The hon. member for Vancouver East knows about them as well as I do. He knows their policy and their approach to industrial relations. He knows they say: "We are not going to obey the law; we are going to take the law into our own hands."
I get tired of hearing people talk so much about rights and not enough about responsibilities. The mere fact that something is put down on paper does not always ensure its application. I have had some experience with the labour movement in this country and in Europe. While I am not going to name countries, I would point out that one of the Balkan countries approved more conventions of the international labour office than any other country in the world. Yet I think it fair to say that industrial conditions in that country were possibly the most backward in Europe. My hon. friend the leader of the Social Credit party read a bill of rights which I think was passed by the legislature of Alberta.

I also hope this parliament will not be satisfied with a mere reiteration of principles of rights, some of which were passed centuries ago, and not in this country at all. While these principles still have a value and we would wish to re-

tain them, yet there are other phases of liberty which we have never tasted and which I conceive should be fundamental in any bill of rights we might draw up.
The minister who has just taken his seat says he believes in what he calls the British way, of not writing it down on paper. I do not think there is any harm in doing that, but of course I agree with him that if that is all you do you are not doing much. But he is in an enviable position. If I were where he is and could write these things into the lives of the Canadian people by actions, I think it would be great; and if he will do that we shall not clamour for any bill of rights whatsoever. I agree that merely declaring something does not make it so. The hon. gentleman to my left has given us an outline of an admirable bill, in sentiment, passed in Alberta. These declarations have some value; they are at least declarations of faith, if nothing else; they are a declaration of the objective a nation sets for itself. But merely to declare that we shall have this liberty and that liberty will not give it.
The main point I wish to make is this. I want to see a bill of rights that will be up to date, that will put into legislation and practice in the economic, social and educational life of Canada those principles of liberty which I think we all conceive to have been the objectives of the men who fought in the last great war. I want to emphasize that the very basis of that must be economic liberty, for there can be no liberty in any country in which one individual must depend for his right to live upon the right of somebody else to hire him. We have seen too much of that kind of bondage. So that whether or not this amendment passes I hope it will not be regarded in this house or in the country as a complete bill of rights. I have the hope, expressed by my hon. friend to my left, that during this or next session a carefully prepared bill of rights will be brought in, which will begin with economic liberty and go on from that to restate in the most modern way possible all the other liberties which flow therefrom.
I believe the instances brought to the attention of this committee by the hon. member for' Spadina are a disgrace to Canada. I hope that those hon. members who heard that will feel as I do about it and protest against it. The circumstances which we all know are prevalent in this country where men cannot find work, where men have not sufficient income to maintain their families and give them an education-all this is a negation of our liberty. A country abounding in wealth as this one is should be ashamed

to know that such things exist. That is something I wanted to emphasize because it is not included in the amendment. A bill of rights should make economic liberty the basis of all liberties we desire to see in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I think in every way this has been a most constructive debate. Apart altogether from the appropriateness of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre in regard to what is in my opinion a most important bill in this Commons of Canada, I think we shall all agree that basically we are not very far apart. I have, as one who was born and bred where freedom had to be fought for, where fredom was denied and defied, heard with some cynicism the nonsense that has been talked in this house about magna charta and the Bill of Rights. After that declaration given to the barons at Runnymede, after the Bill of Rights and the various reforms, everything was broken up by wars of tyranny.
A few years after Runnymede we had to fight at Bannockburn in Scotland in 1314. We had to fight again for our very existence at Flodden in 1513. This, despite all the great charters and rights which you prate of so greatly in this Canada, a country largely made up by those who loved freedom who came from Scotland. The hon. member for Vancouver East reminded this committee of that [DOT] the other evening. His people were the victims of tyranny in the highlands and so were mine. My grandmother's house was burned down because of tyranny and oppression. Where then was your bill of rights? Where then was your Magna Charta? Where then was your declaration of rights?
The hon. member for Vancouver East never said a truer thing in his life than when he said to-night that human rights, political rights and economic rights cannot be defined by charter. Basically and fundamentally they are in the soul and spirit of man. I think everyone of us in this chamber knows a little about the history of Canada. You had to fight in Canada for your rights. You are fighting for your rights to-day in Canada. No one can convince me that because of a matter of procedure which may affect the right of personal and political liberty you are going to destroy the fundamental rights of freedom. A poniard has been planted at the back of our nation, and when that happens it requires drastic remedies. Sometimes we have to sacrifice these personal liberties which may mean so much, and which I think I love as much as anyone, in order to preserve and maintain the freedom and strength of our nation.
You have the rights of the provinces in Canada. You have the rights of the federal authority in Canada. You have economic rights in Canada. You have fundamental human rights. Do you think for one second that this miserable, anaemic amendment meets the fundamental and basic problems of the rights of our people as Canadians, as Liberals, as Conservatives, as socialists or as those who come from Alberta? Like my hon. friend who spoke, I was amazed and ashamed. No one in this house has a higher respect for the hon. member for Peace River than I, but according to our accepted doctrines, what was the most wanton violation of fundamental rights that ever took place in this Dominion of Canada? It was that futile and fatuous measure by the former premier of Alberta who attempted to deprive men of the right of return on proper investment in the province. That may be right; according to the doctrines of the future, Alberta may be right. We are moving fast these days.
British Columbia has denied the franchise to orientals. Others think we are wrong, but we think we are right. Who here says that we are wrong?

Then in a time, not too long away, we can fashion and evolve a declaration of principles if you like-a bill of rights has a somewhat obnoxious significance to my mind because of my little knowledge of old country history-a declaration of Canadian principles containing the real stuff of freedom, the principles for which our people have fought and are now fighting.

There are certain people who are not entitled to have Canadian citizenship, and this committee should bear that fact in mind. The section reads:
A Canadian citizen who, when outside of Canada and not under a disability, by any voluntary and formal act other than marriage, acquires the nationality or citizenship of a country other than Canada shall thereupon cease to be a Canadian citizen.
The provision is that he must do some voluntary and formal act other than marriage. By acquiring the nationality of another country he then will lose his Canadian citizenship. But he can do that only if he is outside Canada; in other words, if he does that act within Canada he cannot be deprived of his citizenship. During a considerable period of this time it was notorious that Roumania was under effective enemy control and influence, although technically neutral. Could this country have tolerated any of her citizens who might be disaffected in relation to the war acquiring, through connivance with the Roumanian government, naturalization as Roumanian citizens? The whole tenor of the discussion thus far has been to emphasize that if Canadian citizens are disloyal or disaffected they should be punished by Canadian authority; in other words, that we should clean our own house. We cannot have in Canada, any more than they can have in any other country of the commonwealth where there are similar provisions, groups of citizens who acquire within Canada the nationality of a foreign country.
I appreciate that the hon. gentleman is addressing himself to another situation, but if we were to accept this amendment it would mean that any group of citizens could at a particular moment denationalize themselves by some act in connivance with a foreign power. No country in the world can afford to allow citizens within its borders to denationalize themselves. While I appreciate the purpose of the amendment, I cannot accept it because of the great abuses which it would provoke, even though unintentionally.
