subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext:
Before we discuss that I wish to give notice of an amendment, which I am asking my colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs to move:
To amend clause 17 by adding thereto as subsection (2) the following:
(2) "Where a Canadian citizen who is under the law of any other country a national or a citizen of that country serves in the armed

forces of such country when it is at war with Canada, he shall thereupon cease to be a Canadian citizen."

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: I move accordingly.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: The amendment will necessitate making the original section 17 subsection 1. Does section 17 as amended by subsection 1 carry?

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: I am coming back to where I stood up a little while ago, and I hope that this time I get the right ball in the right pocket. I do not know whether hon. members play that game or not. What I am anxious to have the Secretary of State do is-and if my memory serves me aright he has not yet done it-to give us his, and therefore the government's view, on this whole question of dual nationality. I realize that in times gone by such a thing has existed. My humble opinion is that it is a complete contradiction in terms. In other words, we have heard recently where a certain person avowed a higher duty or morality or something of that sort to a country other than Canada. Or let us take those, of whom we have quite a number, that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle spoke about a moment ago. There are United States women who have married Canadian husbands. Many of them are now living in Nassau to avoid taxation and that sort of thing; they go freely between California and Canada, and the only way, as I understand it, that they can lose that United States citizenship is if they vote in this country.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: That is one of the ways.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: That is the main way.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: No; there are others.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: I say that is the main way; but we, being opposed in politics, watch that they do not vote, so that it really does not happen very often.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: Maybe they vote on the wrong side.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext:
I have found that out, and I am glad the hon. member supports me in that respect. This is the only time he and I have seen eye-to-eye since I met him, and in spite of that I still like him. Here is my thought: we have all been making speeches as to what an important bill this is, that it is going to give us a status and a standing. I am all for it, and I agree with all that. But as a matter of common sense, is it possible for any person to have two loyalties? Is it possible for any person to take the oath of allegiance to the'

Canadian Citizenship
king and at the same time take the oath of allegiance to the ruling person, or whatever it may be, in another country? It is all very well to say that many of us have not taken the oath of allegiance. I never did until I came to the parliament of Canada. I spoke of being Canadian-born; that is so; nevertheless the same loyalties are required of me, and the same laws apply to me, I mean, with respect to treason, official secrets and acts of that description. Therefore I should like from the Secretary of State his view as to what is the position of a person having dual citizenship. Nationality is the wrong word; it is citizenship. That is what they have. In my judgment it is a complete contradiction in terms and it is just not possible. Let us assume that the woman is a person, as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle so ably reminded us a moment ago. Indeed, her presence would put the question out of debate, and the hon. member is quite a person at that. Will the minister please tell me how a person can be a citizen in two countries having regard to the loyalty to a country which citizenship involves?

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext:
There is actually no difference at all between the hon. gentleman and myself. What we have tried to do, in so far as that is possible, is to avoid as many occasions of dual nationality as we can. Of course, the hon. gentleman is correct; one cannot be really loyal to two countries, particularly when they have opposite currents of political thought, different ideologies and the like. No one quarrels with the hon. gentleman's statement, and all this bill does is to minimize, in comparison with the existing law, the occasions of dual nationality. One of the reasons for the Hague conference of 1930, to which I have made several references, was by agreement to try to get countries to pass laws of nationality which would minimize occasions of dual nationality. It is possible under the existing law in some countries to-day for a person to have no fewer than eleven nationalities. As hon. gentlemen know, before the war, by countries who were our allies and by some who were not, persons who came to this and other countries did not lose the . nationality of these other countries. I do not want to mention specific countries. I have not in mind at the moment the far eastern countries but some European nations. Nationality is' acquired by most countries either through jus soli, the law of the place, or jus sanguinis, the law of blood relationship, or a combination of these two. All that countries can hope to do in the framing of their
nationality laws is to create a situation which will avoid so far as it is possible dual or more than double nationality.
Lawyers in the house will recall the case of an individual born in a zeppelin travelling over the territory of the United States, the father a German and the mother an Italian, creating a situation where that child under the laws of four different countries was a national of as many countries. These are situations that can be cured only by common agreement among the nations. I cannot add anything more. I fully agree with everything the hon. gentleman has said, and we are doing in this bill all we can to minimize occasions of dual nationality.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: I did not intend to speak at all, because I did not think it would require a lot of flowery language to give women the status of human beings, and it seemed to me that the minister was only doing what any decent, self-respecting nation would do sometime in its history, so that it did not require comment. However, for the sake of the hon. gentleman who some time ago wanted to defend the sanctity of the home, I may say that it was called to my attention twenty years ago at a homemakers convention that we had a number of Canadian women who, through marriage had lost their Canadian nationality. They had married aliens and in some cases those aliens were deported because of some criminal offence. Here we had a Canadian woman being deported because her husband was being interned as a criminal in Italy, say, and she knew nothing of Italian, shared no Italian customs or attitudes, and went there as the wife of a criminal. It made her position extremely difficult indeed. I may say for the benefit of the hon. gentleman that women's institutes and councils and organizations, for at least twenty years-because I have been associated with them for twenty years-have tried to establish this simple fact of the integrity of the woman as an individual apart from her husband. We have many cases of United States men coming to this country and living here for many years, enjoying everything but the right to vote, and in spite of such a man's marriage to a Canadian, it has never altered an American's status as a citizen of the republic to the south. I take it that the passing of this bill rescues women from the position to which marriage had degraded them. That is to say, through marriage the woman sank to the level of an imbecile or a dependent. Is that correct?

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext:
It is a fact that under the
old act there were certain classes of disabled persons-idiots, imbeciles, minoi's and women. We have taken women out of that group.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: Do you not include judges?

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: Instead of protecting the sanctity of the home, marriage was degrading it. In other words, the effect of the law was to degrade woman by putting her down to the level of the same status as an imbecile or an incompetent or a minor. The passage of this bill merely restores human rights and allows a woman to choose whether or not she will take the citizenship of her husband, and that, it seems to me, should be a matter between husband and wife. I am all for the sanctity of the home, but not for the sake of taxes-

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: Will the hon. member allow me to interrupt her. It was only her charm that prevented my rising earlier to object on the ground that she was out of order.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: I apologize if I am out of order, and I do not wish any considerations of "charm" to weigh in my favour. I wish to be democratic.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: I take it that the purpose of the amendment which has been introduced is to get at the natural-born Canadian citizen who happens to have another nationality and serves in the armed forces of that nation at a time when that nation is at war with Canada. I take it, in view of the provisions of section 21 (1) (e), it would not be necessary to have such a provision to take care of a naturalized Canadian citizen. Am I right in that assumption?

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: Yes, quite. The section deals with natural-born Canadian citizens.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext:
The amendment, therefore, is designed to make a similar provision in the case of a natural-born Canadian citizen. Would it not be logical to apply the principle of the minister's amendment to the case of a person serving in the armed forces of any country at war with' Canada? Let us take an illustration. Suppose the minister has in mind the case of a natural-born Canadian citizen who, under the law of Japan, because of Japanese origin, is also a subject of the Japanese emperor. Suppose that instead of fighting in the armies of the Japanese emperor he served in a nazi U-boat. Why should he not be under a disability in that case? Why

should he not' lose his Canadian citizenship just as much as if he served in the forces of the Japanese emperor?

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: This deals with a situation that is quite clear; it deals with a man who serves in the armed forces of a country at war with Canada.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: I do not want to belabour the point; it is a simple one. The amendment confines the situation to where a man has served in the armed forces of the other nation which recognizes him as one of its nationals.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: But another nation. The use of the word "such" im the fourth line of the amendment would confine that case to service in the armies of the Japanese emperor. My suggestion is that it be broadened to include any other country which is at war with Canada at the same time. That is in keeping with the principle of the amendment.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: We think this is the proper way to deal with it.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: Is the minister not prepared to take account of the other situation where some person of Japanese origin may be serving in the German armies or in the armies of other nations at war with Canada? Why confine it to the one case where he is serving in the armed forces of a country which looks upon him as a national?

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: Has the minister given consideration to making the provision simply service in a hostile force? Under the law of the enemy country this Canadian citizen might not be a national of that country. I suggest that if he has served in a hostile force he should lose his Canadian citizenship automatically.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext:
Some consideration should be given to that because, according to information given us during the war, a certain number of Japanese left British Columbia, went to Japan, and later went by submarine to Germany where they gave information and assistance before the capitulation. We have no idea as to the number, but the statement has been made by British and prominent Canadians that in Germany there were Japanese who had been born in British Columbia and who were assisting Germany by giving information. I think the minister might well take into consideration what has been brought out by hon. members on the other side.

Where a Canadian citizen serves in the armed forces of any other country when it is at war with Canada he shall thereupon cease to be a Canadian citizen.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: I shall be glad to accept the words:	"any other country".

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: If a Canadian-born citizen who had no other disability of being called another national, but a natural-bom citizen like myself, served outside Canada in an enemy force during the war, and at some future time came back to Canada, would he not be subject to the laws of Canada and be liable to be tried for treason? If we take a person of Japanese or any other origin or nationality that we are talking about at the present time, and if that person served in. the Japanese navy or in a German U-boat and we cancelled his citizenship because of that, does it preclude the possibility of Canada taking action against him for treason or dealing with him as an enemy if he should ever return to Canada, or are we to absolve [DOT] him from that sin and simply punish him by cancelling his citizenship, or are we to use the law of extradition, bring him home and give him the punishment he deserves?

What is the answer to my
question?

Where a Canadian citizen wTho is under the law of any other country a national or citizen of that country serves in the armed forces of any country when it is at war with Canada he shall thereupon cease to be a Canadian citizen.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: That does not answer my question. I should like the minister to deal with my question.

Mr. BENTLEY Will section 25 deal with it after this amendment is passed?

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext:
I wish the Secretary of State would explain what is meant by the inclusion of these words:
. . . who is under the law of any other country a national or citizen of that country.
It seems to me to be redundant. I do not know what the minister is aiming at in including that. Without these words, it would be a plain statement of fact as follows:
Where a Canadian citizen serves in the armed forces of another country when it is at war with Canada he shall thereupon cease to be a Canadian citizen.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: What we are dealing with here is a person who acquires our nationality, and continues to have it and acquires the nationality of another country and serves in the armed forces of that country. The person who does not acquire the nationality of the country in which he is serving is dealt with under our system and in Britain and in Australia and so on in the regular way by using the regular machinery of the courts. He can be found guilty of treason. We are dealing with the special case of a person who is a national of our own country and a national of another country and who at the same time serves in the armed fences of that country when Canada is at war with it. We are dealing with a special group.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: Under this law I do not see how a Japanese who fights in the Japanese forces can be dealt with if he does not return to Canada. That person may claim in Japan that he is a Canadian citizen, and there would be no way of dealing with him if this amendment passes with this wording in it.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: We cannot deal with that situation. What could we do? No law would remedy that.

Mr. Chairman, about a week ago or perhaps longer-we have been so long discussing this bill-I wanted to make some observations on this section but was ruled out of order on a technicality. I wish to take advantage of the opportunity to do so to-night, though I do not believe I can finish before eleven o'clock. Every time we begin to discuss this bill and hon. members from British Columbia take part in the discussion I have to turn to -the front page to assure myself -that it is called the Canadian Citizenship Act, because I believe the bill they are discussing should be entitled 4'the perpetual racial discrimination act." Let me say that I support the amendment. As a matter of fact, knowing as little law as I do, I was in favour of the amendment moved by the hon. member for New Westminster. In the debate on this bill we have witnessed a most curious situation concerning hon. gentlemen to my right. We had the hon. member for Lake Centre and some others attacking the government, particularly the Minister of Justice, most violently in connection with two orders in council which were passed last fall, P.C. 6577 of October 23 and P.C. 6444 of October 5, under whi^h those people caught up in the espionage affair were taken into custody. I have been thinking to myself, what can be said of the sincerity of hon. members who cry to high heaven about the iniquity of those two orders in council, yet forget altogether orders in council, P.C. 7355, 7356 and 7357 which were passed to take away the citizenship rights of not a mere half dozen or so but thousands of Canadian citizens?
. Mr. FULTON: They were not Canadian citizens.
Mr. MacINNIS-: They were.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: The minister just said they were not, when I asked the question.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: The minister did not say anything of the kind, and in any event he can speak for himself. I am saying they were Canadian citizens, and I believe a majority of the court which tried the case said they were.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: And I did not say they were not.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS

I know the minister did not. That is what has gone on in this house day after day for the last three or four weeks.
rMr. Green.]

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: You are not helping it much now.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: I am not helping you people any.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: Nor the debate.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: Certainly I am helping the debate. I am bringing some reason and justice and clarity into it. If we are to deal with the question of citizenship let us deal with the whole question, not citizenship based on some colour or creed or race. For most hon. members from British Columbia the only citizenship worth thinking about, as far as I can ascertain, is trie citizenship of those speaking the English language. Perhaps they would accept the French language as well, because it would be bad politics to exclude it. I should really like to have time to demonstrate to this committee how the hon. member for Lake Centre pummeled the government over these orders in council I have mentioned, P.C. 6577 and 6444, and how skilfully he skated around the other orders in council that were passed, mind you, under far worse conditions than in the case of the other two he mentioned. The National Emergency Powers Act when first introduced provided in section 3(1) (g) for the revocation of naturalization and trie deportation of citizens. That section so outraged the feelings of the people of this country and of the members of this house that they would have nothing to do with it. The bill had to be withdrawn and this obnoxious section, together, with many other obnoxious sections, removed from it. Then, on the second last day of the session, the orders in council providing for the deportation of persons of Japanese origin, many of whom were Canadian citizens, were announced in this house, with not a word of opposition from my hon. friends who are so keen on maintaining the rights of citizenship.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext: You must have been out of the house that day. Read the speeches of the hon. member for Lake Centre.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS

would stretch himself half-way across the floor and say to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, "Are you going to carry out the government's policy in regard to the Japanese?" That government policy was put'into effect by orders in council after this house had rejected it. Either we have to be honest with ourselves, or we cannot be honest with anybody else. You can fool everybody but yourself. You cannot fool yourself; and when you are dishonest with yourself you are dishonest with everybody.
